title: Acute intermittent porphyria – Definition
content: Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP) is a rare autosomal dominant condition caused by a defect in porphobilinogen deaminase, an enzyme involved in the biosynthesis of haem.

title: Acute intermittent porphyria – Pathophysiology
content: In Acute intermittent porphyria, the defect in porphobilinogen deaminase results in the toxic accumulation of delta aminolaevulinic acid and porphobilinogen.

title: Acute intermittent porphyria – Clinical presentation overview
content: Acute intermittent porphyria characteristically presents with abdominal and neuropsychiatric symptoms in 20-40 year olds and is more common in females (5:1).

title: Acute intermittent porphyria – Incidence
content: The incidence of Acute intermittent porphyria is 0.01 cases per 100,000 person-years.

title: Acute intermittent porphyria – Peak incidence age
content: The peak incidence of Acute intermittent porphyria is between 30-40 years of age.

title: Acute intermittent porphyria – Sex ratio
content: Acute intermittent porphyria is more common in females with a sex ratio of 5:1.

title: Acute intermittent porphyria – Abdominal clinical features
content: Abdominal clinical features of Acute intermittent porphyria include abdominal pain and vomiting.

title: Acute intermittent porphyria – Neurological clinical features
content: Neurological clinical features of Acute intermittent porphyria include motor neuropathy.

title: Acute intermittent porphyria – Psychiatric clinical features
content: Psychiatric clinical features of Acute intermittent porphyria include depression.

title: Acute intermittent porphyria – Autonomic clinical features
content: Common autonomic clinical features of Acute intermittent porphyria include hypertension and tachycardia.

title: Acute intermittent porphyria – Urine investigation finding
content: Classically, in Acute intermittent porphyria, urine turns deep red on standing.

title: Acute intermittent porphyria – Urinary porphobilinogen levels
content: Investigations for Acute intermittent porphyria show raised urinary porphobilinogen, which is elevated between attacks and to a greater extent during acute attacks.

title: Acute intermittent porphyria – Porphobilinogen deaminase assay
content: Diagnosis of Acute intermittent porphyria involves an assay of red cells for porphobilinogen deaminase.

title: Acute intermittent porphyria – Serum aminolaevulinic acid and porphobilinogen levels
content: Investigations for Acute intermittent porphyria show raised serum levels of delta aminolaevulinic acid and porphobilinogen.

title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Definition
content: Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) is a malignant disease of the bone marrow arising from myeloid cell lines. Immature cells are released into the blood, impairing normal haematopoiesis and causing anaemia, bleeding, and infections. It is the most common acute leukaemia in adults, with a median age of diagnosis of 65 years. AML is associated with environmental factors, pre-existing haematological disorders, and genetic abnormalities. Diagnosis requires bone marrow biopsy, and treatment involves chemotherapy or haematopoietic cell transplantation. Remission is common, but relapse frequently occurs.

title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Epidemiology
content: The incidence of Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) is 5.00 cases per 100,000 person-years. The peak incidence occurs in individuals aged 70 years and older. AML is more common in males, with a sex ratio of 1.3:1.

title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Aetiology – Genetic Factors
content: Genetic factors contributing to Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) include chromosomal abnormalities such as translocations t(8;21), t(15;17), and t(9;11). Gene mutations impacting cell proliferation and apoptosis, including FLT3, NPM1, and CEBPA, are also significant.

title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Aetiology – Environmental Exposures
content: Environmental exposures linked to Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) include previous chemotherapy or radiation therapy, leading to therapy-related AML. Exposure to benzene and other petrochemicals, as well as ionising radiation, also increases risk.

title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Aetiology – Haematological Disorders
content: Antecedent haematological disorders such as myelodysplastic syndromes and myeloproliferative neoplasms predispose individuals to secondary Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML).

title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Aetiology – Genetic Syndromes
content: Genetic syndromes associated with an increased risk of Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) include Down syndrome, Fanconi anaemia, and Li-Fraumeni syndrome.

title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Pathophysiology – Genetic Mutations
content: Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) arises from genetic mutations in haematopoietic progenitor cells, which disrupt normal cell proliferation and differentiation.

title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Pathophysiology – Blast Accumulation and Bone Marrow Failure
content: The disruption in cell proliferation and differentiation in Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) results in the accumulation of immature cells, known as blasts, in the bone marrow and peripheral blood, ultimately leading to bone marrow failure.

title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Pathophysiology – First Hit Mutation
content: The pathogenesis of Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) often begins with a 'first hit' mutation, such as in FLT3, NPM1, or DNMT3A genes, which confers a proliferative advantage to a haematopoietic stem cell, leading to its clonal expansion.

title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Pathophysiology – Second Hit Mutation
content: A 'second hit' mutation subsequently occurs in Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML), affecting a gene involved in haematopoietic differentiation, such as RUNX1 or CEBPA. This mutation further promotes proliferation and blocks differentiation, leading to the accumulation of immature blasts.

title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Pathophysiology – Blast Accumulation and Cytopenias
content: The accumulation of immature blasts in the bone marrow in Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) suppresses normal haematopoiesis, leading to clinical manifestations such as anaemia, thrombocytopenia, and neutropenia.

title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Pathophysiology – Organ Invasion
content: As Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) progresses, leukaemic blasts can invade other organs, including the spleen, liver, and central nervous system, resulting in organomegaly and other clinical manifestations.

title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Classification – WHO Groups
content: The World Health Organization (WHO) classification system for Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) includes six main groups: AML with recurrent genetic abnormalities, AML with myelodysplasia-related features, Therapy-related AML and MDS, AML not otherwise specified, Myeloid sarcoma, and Myeloid proliferations related to Down syndrome.

title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Classification – FAB Subtypes
content: The French-American-British (FAB) classification system for Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) includes eight subtypes: M0 (acute myeloblastic leukaemia without maturation), M1 (acute myeloblastic leukaemia with minimal granulocyte maturation), M2 (acute myeloblastic leukaemia with granulocyte maturation), M3 (acute promyelocytic leukaemia), M4 (acute myelomonocytic leukaemia), M5 (acute monocytic leukaemia), M6 (acute erythroid leukaemia), and M7 (acute megakaryoblastic leukaemia).

title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Clinical Features – General Presentation
content: Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) typically presents with sudden onset and rapid progression of symptoms. Some patients may be asymptomatic, but common features include pancytopenia, leading to anaemia, bleeding, and infections.

title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Clinical Features – Fever
content: Fever in Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) is mostly due to infections, but can also occur solely due to the leukaemia itself. Immature leucocytes predispose patients to frequent infections.

title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Clinical Features – Anaemia Symptoms
content: Anaemia in Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) can manifest as shortness of breath, palpitations, weakness, fatigue, dizziness, and pallor.

title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Clinical Features – Thrombocytopenia Symptoms
content: Thrombocytopenia in Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) can lead to ecchymoses, petechiae, gingival bleeding, epistaxis, and menorrhagia.

title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Clinical Features – Coagulopathy in APL
content: Coagulopathy is a unique clinical feature of acute promyelocytic leukaemia (APL), a subtype of Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML). It presents as bleeding secondary to disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) and is considered a medical emergency.

title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Clinical Features – Bone Pain
content: Bone pain in Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) can present as sternal discomfort or aching in the extremities, resulting from the expansion of the medullary cavity by the leukaemic process.

title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Clinical Features – Leukaemia Cutis
content: Leukaemia cutis, characterized by nodular, violaceous skin lesions, is observed in up to 13% of Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) patients. It is mostly associated with acute monocytic leukaemia or acute myelomonocytic leukaemia subtypes.

title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Clinical Features – Gingival Hypertrophy
content: Gingival hypertrophy in Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) is primarily associated with the monocytic subtype and is caused by infiltration of leukaemic cells.

title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Clinical Features – CNS Involvement
content: Central nervous system (CNS) involvement in Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) can manifest as headache, visual changes, and nerve palsies. It is mostly associated with acute monocytic leukaemia or acute myelomonocytic leukaemia subtypes.

title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Clinical Features – Organomegaly
content: Organomegaly, including adenopathy, hepatomegaly, and splenomegaly, is an uncommon clinical feature in Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML), occurring in approximately 10% of patients for each. It is caused by the infiltration of leukaemic cells.

title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Investigations – FBC with Differential
content: Full blood count (FBC) with differential in Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) typically shows normocytic, normochromic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, and a leucocyte count that may be low, normal, or raised.

title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Investigations – Peripheral Blood Smear Findings
content: Peripheral blood smear in Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) reveals raised myeloblasts, which are immature cells with large nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and pale blue cytoplasm. Auer rods, pink/red, rod-shaped cytoplasmic granular inclusions that are myeloperoxidase positive and pathognomonic of myeloblasts, are mostly seen with acute promyelocytic leukaemia.

title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Investigations – Coagulation Panel for DIC
content: A coagulation panel for disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) in Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) typically shows raised prothrombin time (PT), raised activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT), low platelet count, elevated D-dimer concentration, and decreased fibrinogen concentration.

title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Investigations – Serum Electrolytes
content: Serum electrolyte abnormalities in Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML), due to increased cell lysis, include hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, hyperkalemia, and hyperuricemia.

title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Investigations – Bone Marrow Aspiration and Biopsy
content: Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy is the confirmatory test for Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML), with a diagnosis established by the presence of ≥ 20% myeloblasts in the bone marrow.

title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Investigations – Immunophenotyping Markers
content: Immunophenotyping in Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) typically shows expression of markers such as CD13, CD33, CD34, CD117, and HLA-DR for the majority of subtypes.

title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Investigations – Cytogenetic Abnormalities
content: Cytogenetic abnormalities in Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) can be identified by conventional karyotypic analysis, reverse transcriptase polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR), or fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH). Specific abnormalities like t(8;21), inv(16), t(16;16), and t(15;17) define AML irrespective of the blast count.

title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Investigations – Molecular Studies
content: Molecular studies in Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) identify abnormalities in specific genes such as FLT3, NPM1, KIT, CEBPA, IDH1, IDH2, p53, or RUNX1.

title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Differential Diagnosis – Acute Lymphocytic Leukaemia
content: Acute lymphocytic leukaemia (ALL) shares similar clinical features with Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML). However, ALL is distinguished by the absence of Auer rods, presence of lymphoblasts, myeloperoxidase negativity, and terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT) positivity.

title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Differential Diagnosis – Myelodysplastic Syndrome
content: Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) presents with anaemia, thrombocytopenia, and infections, similar to Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML). Key differentiating features include blast counts less than 20% and the presence of pseudo-Pelger-Huet abnormality (neutrophils with bilobed nuclei).

title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Differential Diagnosis – Myeloproliferative Neoplasms
content: Myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPN) can present with infections and abnormalities in different cell lines, similar to Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML). However, MPN is characterized by the presence of JAK2 mutation and thrombocytosis.

title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Differential Diagnosis – Chronic Myeloid Leukaemia in Blast Crisis
content: Chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML) in blast crisis can mimic Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) with anaemia, thrombocytopenia, and infections. Differentiation relies on the presence of the Philadelphia chromosome or t(9:22) and raised matured cells in CML.

title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Management – General Principles
content: The general management of Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) involves intensive chemotherapy, with treatment decisions depending on the AML type, prognostic factors, patient comorbidities, age, and preferences. The primary goal for most patients is to achieve complete remission, defined as less than 5% blast cells in the bone marrow or peripheral blood.

title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Management – Acute Promyelocytic Leukaemia (APL)
content: Acute promyelocytic leukaemia (APL), a distinct form of Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML), is a medical emergency. Its treatment differs significantly, utilizing all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) and arsenic to induce the maturation of immature malignant cells.

title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Management – Chemotherapy Agents
content: Chemotherapy for Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) often involves cytarabine and anthracyclines, such as daunorubicin. Targeted agents like midostaurin, ivosidenib, or enasidenib may be added for specific genetic mutations.

title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Management – Induction Chemotherapy
content: Induction chemotherapy in Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) is an intensive combination chemotherapy regimen aimed at achieving complete remission. Failure or relapse may necessitate re-induction therapy.

title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Management – Consolidation Chemotherapy
content: Consolidation chemotherapy for Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) is an intensive treatment administered after complete remission to destroy any remaining tumour cells.

title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Management – Maintenance Chemotherapy
content: Maintenance chemotherapy in Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) is a non-myelosuppressive treatment designed to maintain remission.

title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Management – Haematopoietic Cell Transplantation (HCT)
content: Haematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT) is indicated for Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) patients with unfavourable prognostic factors or those who fail to achieve remission through chemotherapy. Allogeneic HCT is the preferred approach.

title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Management – Supportive Treatment
content: Supportive treatment in Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) includes preventing and treating infections (e.g., antibiotic prophylaxis for febrile neutropenia, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for Pneumocystis pneumonia prophylaxis), immunisations, maintaining hygiene, nutritional support, antiemetics like ondansetron, and transfusions for severe anaemia or thrombocytopenia.

title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Complications – Tumour Lysis Syndrome
content: Tumour lysis syndrome (TLS) is an oncologic emergency in Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML), typically occurring after initiating cytotoxic therapy. Rapid destruction of tumour cells leads to a massive release of intracellular components, causing hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, and hyperuricemia, which can result in acute kidney injury. Clinical features include nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, lethargy, hematuria, seizures, arrhythmias, tetany, muscle cramps, and paresthesia.

title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Complications – Leukostasis
content: Leukostasis in Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) is caused by an excessive number of leukaemic cells (hyperleukocytosis, white blood cell count greater than 50 x 10^9/µL), leading to increased blood viscosity. It typically presents with respiratory or neurological distress, with clinical features such as chest pain, headache, altered mental status, and priapism.

title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Complications – Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC)
content: Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) is a complication of Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML), especially associated with acute promyelocytic leukaemia (APL).

title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Complications – Severe Neutropenia
content: Severe neutropenia, defined as an absolute neutrophil count (ANC) less than 500 cells/µL, is a complication of Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) and carries a high risk of infections.

title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Complications – Severe Thrombocytopenia
content: Severe thrombocytopenia, with platelet counts less than 10,000/µL or active bleeding, is a complication of Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML).

title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Complications – Severe Anaemia
content: Severe anaemia in Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) is typically normocytic and normochromic. A haemoglobin level of ≤8 g/dL necessitates a transfusion.

title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Complications – Venous Thromboembolism
content: Venous thromboembolism is a complication of Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML), mostly occurring during the first three months of treatment.

title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Prognosis – Overview
content: The prognosis of Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) is affected by clinical characteristics and cytogenetic features. The 5-year survival rate is 24%, with improvements in survival time due to advancements in treatment.

title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Prognosis – Favourable Clinical Factors
content: Favourable clinical factors for the prognosis of Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) include age less than 50 years, an ECOG performance status score less than 3 or a Karnofsky score greater than 60%, absence of medical comorbidities, no antecedent haematologic disorder, and no prior exposure to cytotoxic agents or radiation.

title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Prognosis – Favourable Cytogenetic Factors
content: Favourable cytogenetic factors for the prognosis of Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) include an MDR 1-negative phenotype, specific translocations such as t(8;21), inv(16), t(16;16), and t(15;17), as well as NPM1 and CEBPA mutations.

title: Amyloidosis - Definition
content: Amyloidosis is a rare disease characterized by the deposition of abnormal protein called amyloid in various organs and tissues. The amyloid protein can accumulate in any part of the body, including the heart, kidneys, liver, spleen, and nervous system, leading to organ dysfunction and failure. The diagnosis of amyloidosis requires a high index of suspicion and a combination of clinical, laboratory, and imaging tests, as well as tissue biopsy for confirmation.

title: Amyloidosis - Epidemiology
content: The incidence of amyloidosis is 0.80 cases per 100,000 person-years, with a peak incidence between 60-70 years and a 1:1 sex ratio.

title: Amyloidosis - Aetiology
content: The tendency for proteins to fold irregularly and form amyloid fibrils can be increased by a sustained increase in the concentration of the protein due to a pathology, or the presence of an unstable protein with a tendency to fold incorrectly. A combination of environmental and genetic factors is thought to lead to amyloidogenesis.

title: Amyloidosis - AA Subtype Aetiology
content: AA amyloidosis typically results as a complication of severe long-term inflammatory disorders, such as Crohn's disease, rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, malignancies, and conditions predisposing to recurrent infections.

title: Amyloidosis - AL Subtype Aetiology
content: AL amyloidosis usually complicates the excessive proliferation of a single clone of plasma cells and can be associated with multiple myeloma, Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia, or non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

title: Amyloidosis - ATTR Subtype Aetiology
content: ATTR amyloidosis is an autosomal-dominant disease associated with at least 100 different TTR mutations, the most common being the substitution of methionine for valine at position 30.

title: Aplastic anaemia – Definition
content: Aplastic anaemia is a rare, potentially life-threatening haematological condition characterised by pancytopenia and hypocellular bone marrow. It results in insufficiency of all three blood cell lines: erythrocytes, leukocytes, and thrombocytes. The pathophysiology typically involves damage to the pluripotent stem cells leading to bone marrow failure.

title: Aplastic anaemia – Aetiology – Idiopathic
content: Aplastic anaemia can be idiopathic, meaning there is no identifiable cause.

title: Aplastic anaemia – Aetiology – Congenital causes
content: Congenital causes of aplastic anaemia include Fanconi anaemia and dyskeratosis congenita.

title: Aplastic anaemia – Aetiology – Drug-induced causes
content: Drugs such as cytotoxics, chloramphenicol, sulphonamides, phenytoin, and gold can cause aplastic anaemia.

title: Aplastic anaemia – Aetiology – Toxin exposure
content: Exposure to toxins like benzene can lead to aplastic anaemia.

title: Aplastic anaemia – Aetiology – Infectious causes
content: Infections with parvovirus or hepatitis viruses can cause aplastic anaemia.

title: Aplastic anaemia – Aetiology – Radiation exposure
content: Radiation exposure can be an aetiological factor for aplastic anaemia.

title: Aplastic anaemia – Pathophysiology – Core mechanism
content: Aplastic anaemia is characterised by pancytopenia and hypocellular bone marrow, arising from the failure of haematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) within the bone marrow, leading to insufficient production of blood cells.

title: Aplastic anaemia – Pathophysiology – Initial insult to HSCs
content: The initial insult to haematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) or their microenvironment can be mediated by immune mechanisms (cytotoxic T-lymphocytes targeting HSCs) or direct toxic effects from drugs or radiation. Damaged HSCs undergo apoptosis or become senescent.

title: Aplastic anaemia – Pathophysiology – Consequences of HSC failure
content: Diminished HSCs lead to inadequate replenishment of erythrocytes, leukocytes, and thrombocytes. This results in anaemia (fatigue, pallor, dyspnoea), leukocyte depletion (frequent infections), and thrombocytopenia (petechiae, ecchymoses, increased bleeding risk).

title: Aplastic anaemia – Pathophysiology – Bone marrow biopsy findings
content: Bone marrow biopsy in aplastic anaemia typically reveals a hypocellular marrow with fatty infiltration and residual islands of haematopoietic tissue, confirming the diagnosis when correlated with peripheral blood pancytopenia.

title: Aplastic anaemia – Pathophysiology – Molecular mechanisms
content: At a molecular level, mutations in genes like TERT, TERC, and GATA2 may compromise telomere maintenance and genomic stability in HSCs. Autoimmune destruction is facilitated by aberrant expression of antigens on HSCs targeted by autoreactive T-cells.

title: Aplastic anaemia – Pathophysiology – Cytokine dysregulation
content: Cytokine dysregulation, specifically elevated levels of interferon-gamma (IFN-γ) and tumour necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), contributes to suppression of haematopoiesis through induction of apoptosis in progenitor cells.

title: Aplastic anaemia – Classification – Acquired Aplastic Anaemia overview
content: Acquired aplastic anaemia includes idiopathic, drug-induced, chemical exposure, infectious, and radiation-induced causes.

title: Aplastic anaemia – Classification – Acquired Aplastic Anaemia: Idiopathic
content: Idiopathic acquired aplastic anaemia has no identifiable cause and accounts for the majority of cases.

title: Aplastic anaemia – Classification – Acquired Aplastic Anaemia: Drug-induced
content: Drug-induced acquired aplastic anaemia is commonly associated with medications such as chloramphenicol, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), and chemotherapeutic agents.

title: Aplastic anaemia – Classification – Acquired Aplastic Anaemia: Chemical exposure
content: Chemical exposure to substances like benzene and other organic solvents can cause acquired aplastic anaemia.

title: Aplastic anaemia – Classification – Acquired Aplastic Anaemia: Infectious causes
content: Infectious causes of acquired aplastic anaemia include viral infections such as Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), cytomegalovirus (CMV), hepatitis viruses, and HIV.

title: Aplastic anaemia – Classification – Acquired Aplastic Anaemia: Radiation-induced
content: Radiation-induced acquired aplastic anaemia results from ionising radiation exposure.

title: Aplastic anaemia – Classification – Inherited Aplastic Anaemia overview
content: Inherited aplastic anaemia includes Fanconi anaemia, dyskeratosis congenita, Shwachman-Diamond syndrome, and Diamond-Blackfan anaemia.

title: Aplastic anaemia – Classification – Inherited Aplastic Anaemia: Fanconi anaemia
content: Fanconi anaemia is an autosomal recessive disorder characterised by congenital abnormalities, progressive pancytopenia, and increased cancer risk, diagnosed via chromosomal breakage tests.

title: Aplastic anaemia – Classification – Inherited Aplastic Anaemia: Dyskeratosis congenita
content: Dyskeratosis congenita is an X-linked recessive or autosomal dominant disorder involving mutations in telomerase complex genes, presenting with mucocutaneous abnormalities and bone marrow failure.

title: Aplastic anaemia – Classification – Inherited Aplastic Anaemia: Shwachman-Diamond syndrome
content: Shwachman-Diamond syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder featuring exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, skeletal abnormalities, and bone marrow dysfunction, associated with SBDS gene mutations.

title: Aplastic anaemia – Classification – Inherited Aplastic Anaemia: Diamond-Blackfan anaemia
content: Diamond-Blackfan anaemia is a congenital pure red cell aplasia presenting in infancy or early childhood, involving mutations in ribosomal protein genes.

title: Aplastic anaemia – Classification – Severity: Mild
content: Mild aplastic anaemia is defined by bone marrow cellularity 20-30%, absolute neutrophil count (ANC) >1.5 x 10^9/L, platelet count >50 x 10^9/L, and reticulocyte count >60 x 10^9/L.

title: Aplastic anaemia – Classification – Severity: Moderate
content: Moderate aplastic anaemia is defined by bone marrow cellularity 10-20%, ANC 0.5-1.5 x 10^9/L, platelet count 20-50 x 10^9/L, and reticulocyte count 20-60 x 10^9/L.

title: Aplastic anaemia – Classification – Severity: Severe
content: Severe aplastic anaemia is defined by bone marrow cellularity less than 25%, ANC less than 0.5 x 10^9/L, platelet count less than 20 x 10^9/L, and reticulocyte count less than 20 x 10^9/L.

title: Aplastic anaemia – Clinical Features – Haematological findings
content: Clinical features of aplastic anaemia include normochromic, normocytic anaemia, leukopenia (with lymphocytes relatively spared), and thrombocytopenia.

title: Aplastic anaemia – Clinical Features – General presentation
content: The clinical presentation of aplastic anaemia is variable but often includes fatigue (secondary to anaemia), recurrent infections (due to neutropenia) and bleeding tendencies (owing to thrombocytopenia).

title: Aplastic anaemia – Clinical Features – Later developments
content: A minority of patients with aplastic anaemia may later develop paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria or myelodysplasia.

title: Aplastic anaemia – Diagnosis – Confirmation method
content: Diagnosis of aplastic anaemia is confirmed by bone marrow biopsy showing hypocellularity without infiltration by abnormal cells or fibrosis.

title: Aplastic anaemia – Differential Diagnosis – Myelodysplastic Syndrome (MDS)
content: Myelodysplastic Syndrome (MDS) is differentiated from aplastic anaemia by the presence of dysplasia in one or more cell lines and often a hypercellular or normocellular marrow, whereas aplastic anaemia has a hypocellular marrow without dysplasia.

title: Aplastic anaemia – Differential Diagnosis – Paroxysmal Nocturnal Haemoglobinuria (PNH)
content: Paroxysmal Nocturnal Haemoglobinuria (PNH) is differentiated from aplastic anaemia by the presence of episodic haemolysis and confirmed by flow cytometry showing CD55/CD59 deficient red cells.

title: Aplastic anaemia – Differential Diagnosis – Hypoplastic Myelodysplastic Syndrome
content: Hypoplastic Myelodysplastic Syndrome is differentiated from aplastic anaemia by the presence of dysplasia in one or more cell lines, despite a hypocellular marrow.

title: Aplastic anaemia – Management – Supportive Care: Blood products
content: Supportive care for aplastic anaemia includes administration of blood products.

title: Aplastic anaemia – Management – Supportive Care: Infection prevention and treatment
content: Supportive care for aplastic anaemia involves the prevention and treatment of infection.

title: Aplastic anaemia – Management – Immunosuppression: Anti-thymocyte globulin (ATG) and anti-lymphocyte globulin (ALG)
content: Immunosuppression for aplastic anaemia includes Anti-thymocyte globulin (ATG) and anti-lymphocyte globulin (ALG), which are prepared in animals and can cause serum sickness, often requiring steroid cover.

title: Aplastic anaemia – Management – Immunosuppression: Ciclosporin
content: Ciclosporin may also be given as part of immunosuppressive therapy for aplastic anaemia.

title: Aplastic anaemia – Management – Stem Cell Transplantation: Allogeneic transplants
content: Allogeneic stem cell transplantation is a treatment option for aplastic anaemia, with a success rate of up to 80%.

title: Aplastic anaemia – Prognosis – Influencing factors
content: Prognosis for aplastic anaemia depends on several factors including patient age, severity of pancytopenia, response to treatment, and availability of suitable donors for transplantation.

title: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia – Definition
content: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (AIHA) is a condition characterised by the destruction of red blood cells by autoantibodies directed against red blood cell surface antigens.

title: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia – Clinical features
content: Patients with autoimmune haemolytic anaemia may present with symptoms of anaemia such as fatigue and pallor, as well as jaundice due to the breakdown of red blood cells.

title: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia – Investigations
content: The direct Coombs test is a key investigation for autoimmune haemolytic anaemia and will be positive. This test helps to differentiate it from other causes of haemolysis like hereditary spherocytosis.

title: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia – Warm AIHA
content: Warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia is a type of AIHA mediated by IgG antibodies. It is associated with extravascular haemolysis.

title: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia – Cold AIHA
content: Cold autoimmune haemolytic anaemia is a type of AIHA mediated by IgM antibodies. It involves complement-mediated intravascular haemolysis.

title: Beta-thalassaemia – Pathophysiology
content: Beta-thalassaemia major is a severe genetic disorder caused by homozygous mutations in the HBB gene on chromosome 11, leading to a complete absence of beta-globin chain synthesis.

title: Beta-thalassaemia – Clinical Presentation
content: Patients with beta-thalassaemia major are highly symptomatic and require medical intervention, contrasting with the milder beta-thalassaemia trait.

title: Beta-thalassaemia – Prognosis
content: Beta-thalassaemia major is associated with a shortened life expectancy compared to the general population.

title: Beta-thalassaemia trait – Definition
content: Beta-thalassemia trait, also known as beta-thalassemia minor, indicates a patient is a carrier of beta-thalassemia without manifesting the disease itself. It is an inherited blood disorder, present from birth, affecting haemoglobin formation. Symptoms are much milder and complications significantly fewer compared to beta-thalassemia major.

title: Beta-thalassaemia trait – Epidemiology
content: The incidence of beta-thalassemia trait is 1.00 cases per 100,000 person-years, with a peak incidence between 20-30 years. The sex ratio is 1:1.

title: Beta-thalassaemia trait – Aetiology and Risk Factors
content: Beta-thalassemia trait is genetically inherited, requiring at least one parent to have beta-thalassemia or the trait. Inheritance is equal for men and women. It is the most common recessive disease globally, with 1-5% of the world's population being carriers. High-risk ethnic backgrounds include Mediterranean (Italy, Greece, Cyprus, Turkey), South Asian (India, Bangladesh, Pakistan), Middle Eastern, and Chinese/Southeast Asian populations.

title: Beta-thalassaemia trait – Clinical Features
content: Patients with beta-thalassemia trait are typically asymptomatic and show no signs on examination. However, they may develop microcytic and hypochromic anaemia, which can cause fatigue and dyspnoea, particularly during pregnancy due to dilutional anaemia. Beta-thalassemia trait does not progress to beta-thalassemia major and has no other associated health complications.

title: Beta-thalassaemia trait – Pregnancy Complications
content: During pregnancy and labour, patients with beta-thalassemia trait experience a 25% increased rate of anaemia and a 250% increased rate of requiring blood transfusions.

title: Beta-thalassaemia trait – Investigations: NHS Screening Programme
content: The NHS Sickle Cell and Thalassemia (SCT) Screening Programme routinely offers testing for beta-thalassemia trait to pregnant women (antenatal screening) and expectant fathers (if the mother tests positive). In 'high risk' trusts (>=2% positive antenatal screens), all women are tested. In 'low risk' trusts (<1% positive screens), screening is based on FBC, and a Family Origin Questionnaire (FOQ) determines the need for partner testing.

title: Beta-thalassaemia trait – Investigations: General Testing
content: Testing for beta-thalassemia trait can be requested outside antenatal screening via a GP or by self-referral to SCT centres. This is available for both male and female patients and is useful for those with a family history of thalassemia or whose partner has thalassemia.

title: Beta-thalassaemia trait – Investigations: Full Blood Count (FBC) Findings
content: A Full Blood Count (FBC) in beta-thalassemia trait typically shows microcytic anaemia, with normal to moderately low haemoglobin (Hb), low Mean Corpuscular Haemoglobin (MCH) usually 19-23 pg, and low Mean Corpuscular Volume (MCV) usually 60-70 fL.

title: Beta-thalassaemia trait – Investigations: Diagnosis Confirmation
content: Diagnosis of beta-thalassemia trait is confirmed using haemoglobin electrophoresis with quantitation of haemoglobin F (HbF) and A2 (HbA2). Levels of HbA2 are elevated in carriers, ranging from 3.6-7%, compared to 2.2-3.2% in unaffected individuals.

title: Beta-thalassaemia trait – Differential Diagnosis: Iron Deficiency Anaemia
content: Iron deficiency anaemia shares similarities with beta-thalassemia trait, both presenting as microcytic anaemia (low Hb, low Hct). However, iron deficiency anaemia is an acquired condition due to lack of iron, lacks structural abnormality, and has normal HbA2 levels, unlike beta-thalassemia trait.

title: Beta-thalassaemia trait – Differential Diagnosis: Beta-thalassaemia Major
content: Beta-thalassaemia major shares the same genetic mutation on the HBB gene on chromosome 11 with beta-thalassemia trait. However, beta-thalassaemia major is characterized by homozygosity for the mutation, leading to more severe symptoms requiring medical intervention and a shortened life expectancy, unlike the trait.

title: Beta-thalassaemia trait – Differential Diagnosis: Sickle Cell Disease
content: Sickle cell disease is an autosomal recessive haemoglobinopathy that presents as anaemia and is tested for during pregnancy, similar to beta-thalassemia trait. However, sickle cell disease is caused by abnormal haemoglobin S formation, leading to significant complications like painful sickle cell crises and thromboembolism, and more severe anaemia. Its aetiology is also more common in patients from African and Caribbean backgrounds. If a carrier of beta-thalassemia or sickle cell has a child with another haemoglobinopathy carrier, hereditary complications can arise.

title: Beta-thalassaemia trait – Management
content: The majority of patients with beta-thalassemia trait do not require any treatment, and there are no specific treatment guidelines for beta-thalassemia trait.

title: Blood Products: Red Blood Cells - Transfusion in ALL
content: In Acute Lymphoblastic Leukaemia (ALL), red blood cell or platelet transfusions can be used to correct pancytopenia. Prophylactic antibiotics are also considered in cases of severe neutropenia.

title: Blood Products: Red Blood Cells - Transfusion in AML
content: Transfusions are indicated for severe anaemia and thrombocytopenia in the management of Acute Myeloid Leukaemia (AML).

title: Blood Products: Red Blood Cells - Transfusion Threshold in AML
content: In Acute Myeloid Leukaemia (AML), a transfusion is needed for severe normocytic, normochromic anaemia when the haemoglobin level is â‰¤8 g/dL.

title: Blood Products: Red Blood Cells - Transfusion in Hereditary Spherocytosis
content: Red cell transfusions are indicated in severely affected individuals with Hereditary Spherocytosis or during clinical scenarios when they develop anaemia (e.g., during pregnancy or aplastic anaemia). They are not indicated on an ongoing basis due to the risk of iron overload.

title: Burkitt's lymphoma – Clinical features: Abdominal mass and bowel obstruction
content: Burkitt's lymphoma can present with a large abdominal mass and symptoms of bowel obstruction.

title: Burkitt's lymphoma – Investigations: MYC rearrangement by FISH
content: Fluorescence in situ hybridisation (FISH) is used to identify a MYC rearrangement in all individuals newly presenting with histologically high-grade B-cell lymphoma, which includes Burkitt's lymphoma.

title: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia – Asymptomatic presentation
content: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) is often detected incidentally during routine blood tests, with patients having no apparent symptoms.

title: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia – Persistent lymphocytosis
content: The most common finding in Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) is persistent lymphocytosis, often detected during routine blood tests.

title: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia – B symptoms
content: General systemic symptoms, known as B symptoms, including fever, night sweats and weight loss, can occur in Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL). These are less common than in other lymphomas and may indicate a more aggressive disease course.

title: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia – Fatigue
content: Fatigue is a common symptom in Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL), potentially due to anaemia or general malaise associated with the disease.

title: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia – Lymphadenopathy
content: Lymphadenopathy, characterized by painless, firm, rubbery lymph nodes, is a complication of direct tumour infiltration in Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL), most commonly observed in the cervical, axillary, and inguinal regions.

title: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia – Splenomegaly
content: Splenomegaly, presenting with abdominal discomfort and early satiety, is a complication of direct tumour infiltration in Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL).

title: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia – Hepatomegaly
content: Hepatomegaly, though less common than splenomegaly, can occur in Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) due to direct tumour infiltration.

title: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia – Bone marrow infiltration complications
content: Bone marrow infiltration in Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) can lead to complications such as anaemia, thrombocytopenia, and neutropenia.

title: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia – Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (AIHA)
content: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (AIHA), characterized by a positive direct antiglobulin test (DAT), is an autoimmune complication that can occur in Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL).

title: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia – Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP)
content: Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP), characterized by a low platelet count, is an autoimmune complication that can occur in Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL).

title: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia – Pure red cell aplasia (PRCA)
content: Pure red cell aplasia (PRCA), a rare cause of severe anaemia, is an autoimmune complication that can occur in Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL).

title: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia – Acquired von Willebrand disease
content: Acquired von Willebrand disease, a rare bleeding tendency, is an autoimmune complication that can occur in Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL).

title: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia – Full Blood Count (FBC) findings
content: A Full Blood Count (FBC) in suspected Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) typically reveals lymphocytosis (>5 x 10^9/L), which may be accompanied by anaemia or thrombocytopenia in advanced stages. A differential count will show an absolute increase in lymphocytes.

title: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia – Blood Film findings
content: Morphological examination of a peripheral blood smear in Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) can reveal smudge cells, a characteristic feature. However, this finding is not specific and cannot be used alone for diagnosis.

title: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia – Immunophenotyping by Flow Cytometry
content: Immunophenotyping by flow cytometry is the gold standard for diagnosing Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL). Peripheral blood lymphocytes are analysed for expression of various cell surface markers. A typical CLL phenotype shows co-expression of CD19, CD5 and CD23 along with weak expression of surface immunoglobulin and absence or low expression of FMC7 and CD79b.

title: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia – Bone Marrow Aspiration/Biopsy
content: Bone marrow aspiration/biopsy is not necessary for the diagnosis of Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) if flow cytometry is conclusive, but it can provide information about bone marrow infiltration which aids in staging.

title: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia – Cytogenetic Analysis (FISH)
content: Cytogenetic analysis using Fluorescence in situ hybridisation (FISH) can detect chromosomal abnormalities associated with prognosis in Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL). Deletion 17p or TP53 mutation indicates poor prognosis, while deletion 13q as a sole abnormality indicates favourable prognosis.

title: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia – Serum Immunoglobulins
content: Serum immunoglobulin levels should be assessed at diagnosis and monitored during follow-up in Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL), as hypogammaglobulinaemia is common and can contribute to increased susceptibility to infections.

title: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia – Other investigations (not routinely required)
content: Other investigations such as lymph node biopsy, computed tomography (CT) scan, or positron emission tomography (PET) scan may be performed based on individual patient symptoms or disease stage in Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL). However, these are not routinely required for the diagnosis.

title: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia – Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia
content: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (AIHA) in Chronic Lymphocytic Leukaemia is characterised by the destruction of red blood cells by autoantibodies. Patients may present with symptoms of anaemia such as fatigue, pallor, and jaundice.

title: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia – Immune thrombocytopenia
content: Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) in Chronic Lymphocytic Leukaemia involves autoantibodies destroying platelets, leading to thrombocytopenia. This can result in easy bruising, petechiae, or more serious bleeding complications.

title: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia – Recurrent infections due to hypogammaglobulinaemia and neutropenia
content: Patients with Chronic Lymphocytic Leukaemia may experience recurrent infections due to hypogammaglobulinaemia and neutropenia. Infections commonly involve the respiratory tract but can also include herpes zoster reactivation.

title: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia – Richter's transformation
content: Richter's transformation is a rare but serious complication of Chronic Lymphocytic Leukaemia where CLL transforms into an aggressive lymphoma. Patients may present with rapidly enlarging lymph nodes, splenomegaly, and B symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss).

title: Cryoglobulinaemia – Definition
content: Cryoglobulinaemia is a family of rare conditions characterized by the presence of cryoglobulins in the blood. It is a type of vasculitis, causing irritation and inflammation of blood vessels.

title: Cryoglobulinaemia – Cryoglobulins
content: Cryoglobulins are atypical proteins in the blood that may clump together at body temperatures below 98.6 F (37 C). These clumps can block blood flow, damaging the skin, joints, nerves, kidneys, and liver.

title: Cryoglobulinaemia – Type 1
content: Type 1 cryoglobulinaemia involves one kind of monoclonal atypical protein and is most often linked to blood cancers.

title: Cryoglobulinaemia – Type 2
content: Type 2 cryoglobulinaemia involves both monoclonal and polyclonal atypical proteins and is most often linked to hepatitis C virus.

title: Cryoglobulinaemia – Type 3
content: Type 3 cryoglobulinaemia involves a mix of polyclonal proteins and is most often linked to autoimmune diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis.

title: Cryoglobulinaemia – General Symptoms
content: Some individuals with cryoglobulinaemia may experience no symptoms, while for others, symptoms might come and go.

title: Cryoglobulinaemia – Cutaneous Manifestations
content: Cutaneous manifestations of cryoglobulinaemia include purple skin spots (lesions), which may appear black or brown on darker skin, open leg sores (ulcers), purpura, and Raynaud's phenomenon.

title: Cryoglobulinaemia – Joint Pain
content: Joint pain, similar to that experienced in rheumatoid arthritis, is a common symptom of cryoglobulinaemia.

title: Cryoglobulinaemia – Peripheral Neuropathy
content: Cryoglobulinaemia can cause peripheral neuropathy, damaging nerves in the fingers and toes, leading to numbness and other neurological problems.

title: Cryoglobulinaemia – Causes: Infections
content: Cryoglobulinaemia has been linked to various infections, most commonly Hepatitis C, but also Hepatitis B, HIV, Epstein-Barr, toxoplasmosis, and malaria.

title: Cryoglobulinaemia – Causes: Cancers
content: Certain blood cancers, such as multiple myeloma, Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia, and chronic lymphocytic leukemia, can cause cryoglobulinaemia.

title: Cryoglobulinaemia – Causes: Autoimmune Diseases
content: Autoimmune diseases, where the immune system mistakenly attacks healthy tissues, increase the risk of cryoglobulinaemia. Examples include lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, and Sjogren syndrome.

title: Cryoglobulinaemia – Risk Factors: Sex and Age
content: Cryoglobulinaemia occurs more frequently in women than in men, and symptoms most often begin in middle age.

title: Cryoglobulinaemia – Risk Factors: Associated Diseases
content: Cryoglobulinaemia is linked with diseases such as hepatitis C, HIV, multiple myeloma, Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia, lupus, and Sjogren syndrome.

title: Cryoglobulinaemia – Renal Complications
content: Cryoglobulinaemia can affect the kidneys, leading to symptoms such as protein or blood in the urine, high blood pressure, glomerulonephritis, and potentially kidney failure.

title: Cryoglobulinaemia – Extremity Complications
content: Complications affecting the extremities due to cryoglobulinaemia include ulcers or gangrene.

title: Cryoprecipitate - Composition
content: Cryoprecipitate is a plasma-derived blood product rich in clotting factors, containing Factor VIII, fibrinogen, von Willebrand factor (vWF), and Factor XIII.

title: Cryoprecipitate - Indications
content: Cryoprecipitate is primarily indicated for the replacement of fibrinogen in cases of acquired or congenital deficiency, such as in disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) or massive haemorrhage, particularly when fibrinogen levels are critically low.

title: Disseminated intravascular coagulation – Pathophysiology
content: Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) is a pathological process characterized by the widespread activation of the coagulation cascade, leading to the formation of microthrombi in small and medium-sized vessels throughout the body. This process consumes coagulation factors and platelets, which can lead to a paradoxical state of both thrombosis and hemorrhage. The activation of the coagulation cascade is often triggered by the release of tissue factor into the circulation.

title: Disseminated intravascular coagulation – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Common causes of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) include sepsis (particularly with gram-negative bacteria), severe trauma (such as major crush injuries or burns), obstetric complications (like amniotic fluid embolism or abruptio placentae), and malignancies (especially adenocarcinomas and acute promyelocytic leukaemia).

title: Disseminated intravascular coagulation – Investigations
content: The diagnosis of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) is based on a combination of clinical findings and laboratory tests. Key laboratory findings include thrombocytopenia (low platelet count), prolonged prothrombin time (PT) and activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT), low levels of fibrinogen, and elevated levels of fibrin degradation products (FDPs) and D-dimer. The peripheral blood smear may show schistocytes (fragmented red blood cells).

title: Factor V Leiden – Definition
content: Factor V Leiden is the most common inherited thrombophilia, affecting 5% of the UK population.

title: Factor V Leiden – Pathophysiology
content: Factor V Leiden is characterized by activated protein C resistance.

title: Factor V Leiden – Risk (heterozygous)
content: Individuals heterozygous for Factor V Leiden have a 4-5 times increased risk of thrombosis.

title: Factor V Leiden – Risk (homozygous)
content: Individuals homozygous for Factor V Leiden have a 10 times increased risk of thrombosis.

title: Factor V Leiden – Screening recommendations
content: Screening recommendations exist for Factor V Leiden.

topic: Deep vein thrombosis: diagnosis and management
title: Two-level DVT Wells score
content: The two-level DVT Wells score is a clinical decision rule used to estimate the pre-test probability of deep vein thrombosis. A score of 2 or more is considered 'DVT likely', while a score of 1 or less is considered 'DVT unlikely'.

topic: Deep vein thrombosis: diagnosis and management
title: Investigation of suspected DVT
content: If DVT is likely (Wells score >= 2), a proximal leg vein ultrasound scan should be performed within 4 hours. If the scan is negative, a D-dimer test is performed. If DVT is unlikely (Wells score <= 1), a D-dimer test is performed first. If the D-dimer is positive, a proximal leg vein ultrasound is performed.

topic: Deep vein thrombosis: diagnosis and management
title: Anticoagulation
content: Initial treatment for DVT is with a direct-acting oral anticoagulant (DOAC) such as apixaban or rivaroxaban. Low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) is an alternative. The duration of anticoagulation is typically 3 months for a provoked DVT and 6 months for an unprovoked DVT.

content: Target cells are a pathological red cell form seen in sickle-cell anaemia.

title: Beta-thalassaemia – Target cells
content: Target cells are a pathological red cell form seen in beta-thalassaemia.

title: Iron deficiency anaemia – Target cells
content: Target cells are a pathological red cell form seen in iron deficiency anaemia.

content: 'Tear-drop' poikilocytes are a pathological red cell form seen in myelofibrosis.

title: Hereditary spherocytosis – Spherocytes
content: Spherocytes are a pathological red cell form seen in hereditary spherocytosis.

title: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia – Spherocytes
content: Spherocytes are a pathological red cell form seen in autoimmune haemolytic anaemia.

title: Lead poisoning – Basophilic stippling
content: Basophilic stippling is a pathological red cell form seen in lead poisoning.

title: Beta-thalassaemia – Basophilic stippling
content: Basophilic stippling is a pathological red cell form seen in beta-thalassaemia.

title: Sideroblastic anaemia – Basophilic stippling
content: Basophilic stippling is a pathological red cell form seen in sideroblastic anaemia.

title: Myelodysplastic syndrome – Basophilic stippling
content: Basophilic stippling is a pathological red cell form seen in myelodysplastic syndrome.

title: G6PD deficiency – Heinz bodies
content: Heinz bodies are a pathological red cell form seen in G6PD deficiency.

title: Disseminated intravascular coagulation – Schistocytes ('helmet cells')
content: Schistocytes ('helmet cells') are a pathological red cell form seen in disseminated intravascular coagulation.

title: Iron deficiency anaemia – 'Pencil' poikilocytes
content: 'Pencil' poikilocytes are a pathological red cell form seen in iron deficiency anaemia.

title: Macrocytic anaemia – Hypersegmented neutrophils
content: Hypersegmented neutrophils are an abnormality seen in megaloblastic anaemia, which is a type of macrocytic anaemia.

title: Transfusion reactions – Classification
content: Blood product transfusion complications may be broadly classified into immunological (acute haemolytic, non-haemolytic febrile, allergic/anaphylaxis), infective, transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI), transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO), and other (hyperkalaemia, iron overload, clotting) reactions.

title: Transfusion reactions – Non-haemolytic febrile reaction Aetiology
content: Non-haemolytic febrile reactions are thought to be caused by antibodies reacting with white cell fragments in the blood product and cytokines that have leaked from the blood cell during storage. They are also due to white blood cell HLA antibodies, often the result of sensitization by previous pregnancies or transfusions.

title: Transfusion reactions – Non-haemolytic febrile reaction Clinical features
content: Clinical features of a non-haemolytic febrile reaction include fever and chills.

title: Transfusion reactions – Non-haemolytic febrile reaction Epidemiology
content: Non-haemolytic febrile reactions occur in 1-2% of red cell transfusions and 10-30% of platelet transfusions.

title: Transfusion reactions – Non-haemolytic febrile reaction Management
content: Management of a non-haemolytic febrile reaction involves slowing or stopping the transfusion, administering paracetamol, and monitoring the patient.

title: Transfusion reactions – Minor allergic reaction Aetiology
content: Minor allergic reactions are thought to be caused by foreign plasma proteins.

title: Transfusion reactions – Minor allergic reaction Clinical features
content: Clinical features of a minor allergic reaction include pruritus and urticaria.

title: Transfusion reactions – Minor allergic reaction Management
content: Management of a minor allergic reaction involves temporarily stopping the transfusion, administering an antihistamine, and monitoring the patient. If symptoms resolve, the transfusion may be continued.

title: Transfusion reactions – Anaphylaxis Aetiology
content: Anaphylaxis can be caused by patients with IgA deficiency who have anti-IgA antibodies.

title: Transfusion reactions – Anaphylaxis Clinical features
content: Clinical features of anaphylaxis include hypotension, dyspnoea, wheezing, and angioedema. Symptoms typically arise within minutes of starting the transfusion.

title: Transfusion reactions – Anaphylaxis Management
content: Management of anaphylaxis involves immediately and permanently stopping the transfusion, administering intramuscular adrenaline, providing ABC support, oxygen, and fluids. Antihistamines, corticosteroids, and bronchodilators should also be considered.

title: Transfusion reactions – Acute haemolytic reaction Aetiology
content: Acute haemolytic transfusion reaction results from an ABO blood group mismatch, usually due to human error, causing massive intravascular haemolysis by IgM-type antibodies.

title: Transfusion reactions – Acute haemolytic reaction Clinical features
content: Symptoms of an acute haemolytic reaction begin minutes after transfusion starts and include fever, abdominal pain, chest pain, agitation, and hypotension.

title: Transfusion reactions – Acute haemolytic reaction Management
content: Treatment for an acute haemolytic reaction includes immediate transfusion termination, generous fluid resuscitation with saline solution, and informing the lab. Complications include disseminated intravascular coagulation and renal failure.

title: Transfusion reactions – Acute haemolytic reaction Investigations
content: To confirm diagnosis of an acute haemolytic reaction, check the identity of the patient/name on the blood product, and send blood for a direct Coombs test, repeat typing, and cross-matching.

title: Transfusion reactions – Transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO) Aetiology
content: Transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO) is caused by an excessive rate of transfusion or pre-existing heart failure.

title: Transfusion reactions – Transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO) Clinical features
content: Clinical features of transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO) include pulmonary oedema and hypertension. This is a key difference from TRALI.

title: Transfusion reactions – Transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO) Management
content: Management of transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO) involves slowing or stopping the transfusion, and considering intravenous loop diuretics (e.g., furosemide) and oxygen.

title: Transfusion reactions – Transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI) Pathophysiology
content: Transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI) is a non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema thought to be secondary to increased vascular permeability caused by host neutrophils that become activated by substances in donated blood.

title: Transfusion reactions – Transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI) Clinical features
content: Transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI) is characterized by the development of hypoxaemia/acute respiratory distress syndrome within 6 hours of transfusion. Features include hypoxia, pulmonary infiltrates on chest x-ray, fever, and hypotension.

title: Transfusion reactions – Transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI) Management
content: Management of transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI) involves stopping the transfusion, providing oxygen, and supportive care.

title: Transfusion reactions – Infective complications
content: Infective complications of blood transfusions include bacterial and viral transmissions. The risk varies with blood product type, storage conditions, components, and duration of storage.

title: Transfusion reactions – Red Blood Cell (RBC) Infective complications
content: Red Blood Cells (RBCs) are primarily at risk for transmitting viral agents such as HIV, HBV, and HCV. Bacterial contamination is less common but possible, particularly from skin flora during collection. Viral infections can lead to chronic disease states such as chronic hepatitis or AIDS, while bacterial infections may manifest as sepsis.

title: Transfusion reactions – Platelet Infective complications
content: Platelets are stored at room temperature, increasing the risk of bacterial proliferation. Common contaminants include Staphylococcus epidermidis and Bacillus cereus. Bacterial contamination of platelets is more likely to lead to rapid onset of sepsis and septic shock.

title: Transfusion reactions – Prion transmission (vCJD)
content: Although the absolute risk is very small, variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (vCJD) may be transmitted via blood transfusion. Steps taken to minimize this risk include leucodepletion of all donations since late 1999, fractionation of plasma derivatives from imported plasma since 1999, and exclusion of blood component recipients from donating blood since 2004.

title: Blood products – CMV transmission
content: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is transmitted in leucocytes.

title: Blood products – Leucocyte depletion
content: Most blood products (except granulocyte transfusions) are now leucocyte depleted.

title: Blood products – Requirement for CMV negative blood
content: CMV negative products are rarely required due to leucocyte depletion.

title: Blood products – Irradiated blood composition
content: Irradiated blood products are depleted of T-lymphocytes.

title: Blood products – Purpose of irradiated blood
content: Irradiated blood products are used to avoid transfusion-associated graft versus host disease (TA-GVHD).

title: Graft versus host disease – Cause of TA-GVHD
content: Transfusion-associated graft versus host disease (TA-GVHD) is caused by engraftment of viable donor T lymphocytes.

title: Blood products – Indications for CMV negative blood: Granulocyte transfusions
content: CMV negative blood is indicated for granulocyte transfusions.

title: Blood products – Indications for CMV negative blood: Intra-uterine transfusions
content: CMV negative blood is indicated for intra-uterine transfusions.

title: Blood products – Indications for CMV negative blood: Neonates
content: CMV negative blood is indicated for neonates up to 28 days post expected date of delivery.

title: Blood products – Indications for CMV negative blood: Pregnancy
content: CMV negative blood is indicated for elective transfusions during pregnancy (not during labour or delivery).

title: Blood products – Indications for Irradiated blood: Granulocyte transfusions
content: Irradiated blood is indicated for granulocyte transfusions.

title: Blood products – Indications for Irradiated blood: Intra-uterine transfusions
content: Irradiated blood is indicated for intra-uterine transfusions.

title: Blood products – Indications for Irradiated blood: Neonates
content: Irradiated blood is indicated for neonates up to 28 days post expected date of delivery.

title: Blood products – Indications for Irradiated blood: Bone marrow/stem cell transplants
content: Irradiated blood is indicated for bone marrow / stem cell transplants.

title: Blood products – Indications for Irradiated blood: Immunocompromised patients
content: Irradiated blood is indicated for immunocompromised patients (e.g., chemotherapy or congenital).

title: Blood products – Indications for Irradiated blood: Hodgkin lymphoma
content: Irradiated blood is indicated for patients with or previous Hodgkin lymphoma.

title: Fresh Frozen Plasma – Indications
content: Fresh frozen plasma (FFP) is most suited for 'clinically significant' but without 'major haemorrhage' in patients with a prothrombin time (PT) ratio or activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) ratio > 1.5.

title: Fresh Frozen Plasma – Volume
content: Fresh frozen plasma (FFP) is typically administered in volumes of 150-220 mL.

title: Fresh Frozen Plasma – Prophylactic Use
content: Fresh frozen plasma (FFP) can be used prophylactically in patients undergoing invasive surgery where there is a risk of significant bleeding.

title: Fresh Frozen Plasma – Universal Donor
content: The universal donor of Fresh Frozen Plasma (FFP) is AB blood because it lacks any anti-A or anti-B antibodies.

title: Cryoprecipitate – Composition and Primary Use
content: Cryoprecipitate contains concentrated Factor VIII:C, von Willebrand factor, fibrinogen, Factor XIII and fibronectin, and is most commonly used to replace fibrinogen.

title: Cryoprecipitate – Volume
content: Cryoprecipitate is administered in a much smaller volume than FFP, typically 15-20mL.

title: Cryoprecipitate – Indications (Fibrinogen Concentration)
content: Cryoprecipitate is most suited for patients with 'clinically significant' bleeding but without 'major haemorrhage' who have a fibrinogen concentration < 1.5 g/L.

title: Cryoprecipitate – Example Use Cases
content: Example use cases for cryoprecipitate include disseminated intravascular coagulation, liver failure, hypofibrinogenaemia secondary to massive transfusion, emergency situations for haemophiliacs (when specific factors are not available), and von Willebrand disease.

title: Cryoprecipitate – Prophylactic Use (Surgery)
content: Cryoprecipitate can be used prophylactically in patients undergoing invasive surgery where there is a risk of significant bleeding and the fibrinogen concentration is < 1.0 g/L.

title: Prothrombin Complex Concentrate – Emergency Reversal
content: Prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) is used for the emergency reversal of anticoagulation in patients with either severe bleeding or a head injury with suspected intracerebral haemorrhage.

title: Prothrombin Complex Concentrate – Prophylactic Use (Surgery)
content: Prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) can be used prophylactically in patients undergoing emergency surgery depending on the particular circumstance.

title: Haematology – DOAC Indications: Stroke prevention in non-valvular AF
content: Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) are used for the prevention of stroke in non-valvular AF. NICE stipulate that certain other risk factors should be present, including prior stroke or transient ischaemic attack, age 75 years or older, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, or heart failure.

title: Venous thromboembolism – DOAC Indications: Post-surgical VTE prevention
content: Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) are used for the prevention of venous thromboembolism (VTE) following hip/knee surgery.

title: Deep vein thrombosis – DOAC Indications: Treatment of DVT and PE
content: Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) are used for the treatment of deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism (PE).

title: Haematology – Dabigatran: Mechanism and Excretion
content: Dabigatran is a direct thrombin inhibitor and is majority renal excreted.

title: Haematology – Rivaroxaban: Mechanism and Excretion
content: Rivaroxaban is a direct factor Xa inhibitor and is majority liver excreted.

title: Haematology – Apixaban: Mechanism and Excretion
content: Apixaban is a direct factor Xa inhibitor and is majority faecal excreted.

title: Haematology – Edoxaban: Mechanism and Excretion
content: Edoxaban is a direct factor Xa inhibitor and is majority faecal excreted.

title: Haematology – Dabigatran: Reversal Agent
content: The reversal agent for Dabigatran is Idarucizumab.

title: Haematology – Rivaroxaban: Reversal Agent
content: The reversal agent for Rivaroxaban is Andexanet alfa.

title: Haematology – Apixaban: Reversal Agent
content: The reversal agent for Apixaban is Andexanet alfa.

title: Haematology – Edoxaban: Reversal Agent
content: There is no authorised reversal agent for Edoxaban, although andexanet alfa has been studied. Prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) is often used in clinical practice.

title: Graft versus host disease – Definition
content: Graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) is a serious complication of allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT). It occurs when donor T cells attack recipient tissues due to immunogenetic differences.

title: Graft versus host disease – Distinction from Transplant Rejection
content: Graft-versus-host disease is distinct from transplant rejection, where the recipient’s immune system attacks the donor tissue.

title: Graft versus host disease – Other Occurrences
content: GVHD may also occur after solid organ transplantation or blood transfusion in immunocompromised patients.

title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) is associated with Hodgkin's lymphoma.

title: Burkitt's lymphoma – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) is associated with Burkitt's lymphoma.

title: Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Human Immunodeficiency Virus type 1 (HIV-1) is associated with high-grade B-cell lymphoma, a type of Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma.

title: Haemolytic anaemias – Hereditary causes
content: Hereditary haemolytic anaemias can be subdivided into membrane, metabolism or haemoglobin defects.

title: Hereditary spherocytosis – Cause of haemolytic anaemia
content: Hereditary spherocytosis is a membrane defect that causes hereditary haemolytic anaemia.

title: G6PD deficiency – Cause of haemolytic anaemia
content: G6PD deficiency is a metabolism defect that causes hereditary haemolytic anaemia.

title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Cause of haemolytic anaemia
content: Sickle cell anaemia is a haemoglobinopathy that causes hereditary haemolytic anaemia.

title: Beta-thalassaemia – Cause of haemolytic anaemia
content: Thalassaemia is a haemoglobinopathy that causes hereditary haemolytic anaemia.

title: Haemolytic anaemias – Acquired causes
content: Acquired haemolytic anaemias can be subdivided into immune (Coombs-positive) and non-immune (Coombs-negative) causes.

title: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia – Immune cause
content: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (warm/cold antibody type) is an immune (Coombs-positive) cause of acquired haemolytic anaemia.

title: Transfusion reactions – Immune cause of haemolytic anaemia
content: Transfusion reaction (alloimmune) is an immune (Coombs-positive) cause of acquired haemolytic anaemia.

title: Drug-induced haemolytic anaemia – Immune cause
content: Drugs like methyldopa and penicillin can cause immune (Coombs-positive) acquired haemolytic anaemia.

title: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura – Non-immune cause of haemolytic anaemia
content: Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (MAHA), including TTP/HUS, is a non-immune (Coombs-negative) cause of acquired haemolytic anaemia.

title: Disseminated intravascular coagulation – Non-immune cause of haemolytic anaemia
content: Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (MAHA), including DIC, is a non-immune (Coombs-negative) cause of acquired haemolytic anaemia.

title: Malignancy – Non-immune cause of haemolytic anaemia
content: Malignancy can cause microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (MAHA), a non-immune (Coombs-negative) acquired haemolytic anaemia.

title: Pre-eclampsia – Non-immune cause of haemolytic anaemia
content: Pre-eclampsia can cause microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (MAHA), a non-immune (Coombs-negative) acquired haemolytic anaemia.

title: Prosthetic heart valves – Non-immune cause of haemolytic anaemia
content: Prosthetic heart valves are a non-immune (Coombs-negative) cause of acquired haemolytic anaemia.

title: Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria – Non-immune cause of haemolytic anaemia
content: Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria is a non-immune (Coombs-negative) cause of acquired haemolytic anaemia.

title: Malaria – Non-immune cause of haemolytic anaemia
content: Infections like malaria are a non-immune (Coombs-negative) cause of acquired haemolytic anaemia.

title: Drug-induced haemolytic anaemia – Non-immune cause
content: Drugs like dapsone can cause non-immune (Coombs-negative) acquired haemolytic anaemia.

title: Zieve syndrome – Definition
content: Zieve syndrome is a rare clinical syndrome of Coombs-negative haemolysis, cholestatic jaundice, and transient hyperlipidaemia associated with heavy alcohol use, typically following a binge.

title: Zieve syndrome – Management
content: Zieve syndrome typically resolves with abstinence from alcohol.

title: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (AIHA) is most commonly idiopathic but may be secondary to a lymphoproliferative disorder, infection or drugs.

title: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia – Investigations (General features)
content: General features of haemolytic anaemia: anaemia, reticulocytosis, low haptoglobin, raised lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and indirect bilirubin.

title: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia – Investigations (Blood film)
content: Blood film: spherocytes and reticulocytes.

title: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia – Investigations (Specific feature)
content: Specific features of autoimmune haemolytic anaemia: positive direct antiglobulin test (Coombs' test).

title: Warm AIHA – Pathophysiology
content: In warm AIHA the antibody (usually IgG) causes haemolysis best at body temperature and haemolysis tends to occur in extravascular sites, for example the spleen.

title: Warm AIHA – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Causes of warm AIHA: idiopathic, autoimmune disease (e.g. systemic lupus erythematosus), neoplasia, lymphoma, chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, drugs (e.g. methyldopa).

title: Warm AIHA – Management
content: Management of warm AIHA: treatment of any underlying disorder, steroids (+/- rituximab) are generally used first-line.

title: Cold AIHA – Pathophysiology
content: The antibody in cold AIHA is usually IgM and causes haemolysis best at 4 deg C. Haemolysis is mediated by complement and is more commonly intravascular.

title: Cold AIHA – Clinical features
content: Features of cold AIHA may include symptoms of Raynaud's and acrocynaosis.

title: Cold AIHA – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Causes of cold AIHA: neoplasia (e.g. lymphoma), infections (e.g. mycoplasma, EBV).

title: Cold AIHA – Management
content: Patients with cold AIHA respond less well to steroids.

title: Hereditary angioedema – Definition
content: Hereditary angioedema (HAE) is an autosomal dominant condition associated with low plasma levels of the C1 inhibitor (C1-INH, C1 esterase inhibitor) protein.

title: Hereditary angioedema – Pathophysiology
content: C1 inhibitor (C1-INH) is a multifunctional serine protease inhibitor; the probable mechanism behind attacks in Hereditary angioedema is uncontrolled release of bradykinin resulting in oedema of tissues.

title: Hereditary angioedema – Investigations
content: During an attack of Hereditary angioedema, the C1 inhibitor (C1-INH) level is low.

title: Hereditary spherocytosis – Definition
content: Hereditary spherocytosis is the most common hereditary haemolytic anaemia in people of northern European descent.

title: Hereditary spherocytosis – Pathophysiology - Genetic basis
content: Hereditary spherocytosis is caused by autosomal dominant mutations affecting proteins that anchor the cytoskeleton to the plasma membrane, such as spectrin.

title: Hereditary spherocytosis – Pathophysiology - Red blood cell morphology
content: In hereditary spherocytosis, the normal biconcave disc shape of red blood cells is replaced by a sphere-shaped red blood cell.

title: Hereditary spherocytosis – Pathophysiology - Red blood cell destruction
content: Red blood cell survival is reduced in hereditary spherocytosis as they are destroyed by the spleen.

title: Hereditary spherocytosis – Pathophysiology - Splenic trapping
content: Spherocytes in hereditary spherocytosis cannot deform adequately to traverse the splenic cords, leading to them becoming trapped and destroyed by splenic macrophages (extravascular haemolysis).

title: Hereditary spherocytosis – Clinical features - Failure to thrive
content: Patients with hereditary spherocytosis may present with failure to thrive.

title: Hereditary spherocytosis – Clinical features - Jaundice
content: Jaundice can be a clinical feature of hereditary spherocytosis.

title: Hereditary spherocytosis – Clinical features - Gallstones
content: Gallstones can be a clinical feature of hereditary spherocytosis.

title: Hereditary spherocytosis – Clinical features - Splenomegaly
content: Splenomegaly is a common clinical feature in hereditary spherocytosis.

title: Hereditary spherocytosis – Clinical features - Aplastic crisis
content: An aplastic crisis precipitated by parvovirus infection can occur in hereditary spherocytosis.

title: Hereditary spherocytosis – Clinical features - Haemolysis variability
content: The degree of haemolysis in hereditary spherocytosis is variable.

title: Hereditary spherocytosis – Clinical features - MCHC
content: In hereditary spherocytosis, the Mean Corpuscular Haemoglobin Concentration (MCHC) is elevated.

title: Hereditary spherocytosis – Diagnosis - Osmotic fragility test
content: The osmotic fragility test was previously recommended for diagnosing hereditary spherocytosis but is now deemed unreliable and no longer recommended.

title: Hereditary spherocytosis – Diagnosis - BJH guidelines for typical cases
content: The British Journal of Haematology (BJH) guidelines state that patients with a family history of Hereditary Spherocytosis (HS), typical clinical features (spherocytes, raised MCHC, increased reticulocytes) do not require any additional tests for diagnosis.

title: Hereditary spherocytosis – Diagnosis - BJH guidelines for equivocal cases
content: If the diagnosis of hereditary spherocytosis is equivocal, the British Journal of Haematology (BJH) recommends the EMA binding test and the cryohaemolysis test.

title: Hereditary spherocytosis – Diagnosis - Atypical presentations
content: For atypical presentations of hereditary spherocytosis, electrophoresis analysis of erythrocyte membranes is the method of choice.

title: Hereditary spherocytosis – Management - Acute haemolytic crisis
content: During an acute haemolytic crisis in hereditary spherocytosis, treatment is generally supportive, and transfusion may be necessary.

title: Hereditary spherocytosis – Management - Folate replacement
content: Longer-term management for hereditary spherocytosis includes folate replacement.

title: Hereditary spherocytosis – Management - Splenectomy
content: Splenectomy is a longer-term treatment option for hereditary spherocytosis.

title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Definition
content: Hodgkin's lymphoma is a malignant proliferation of lymphocytes characterised by the presence of the Reed-Sternberg cell. It has a bimodal age distribution, being most common in the third and seventh decades.

title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Histological Classification: Nodular Sclerosing
