content: Nodular sclerosing is the most common histological type of Hodgkin's lymphoma, accounting for around 70% of cases. It is associated with a good prognosis, is more common in women, and is characterised by lacunar cells.

title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Histological Classification: Mixed Cellularity
content: Mixed cellularity accounts for around 20% of Hodgkin's lymphoma cases. It is associated with a good prognosis and a large number of Reed-Sternberg cells.

title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Histological Classification: Lymphocyte Predominant
content: Lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin's lymphoma accounts for around 5% of cases and is associated with the best prognosis.

title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Histological Classification: Lymphocyte Depleted
content: Lymphocyte depleted Hodgkin's lymphoma is rare and is associated with the worst prognosis.

title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Prognosis: 'B' Symptoms
content: The presence of 'B' symptoms implies a poor prognosis in Hodgkin's lymphoma. These symptoms include weight loss > 10% in the last 6 months, fever > 38ºC, and night sweats.

title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Prognosis: Age
content: Age > 45 years is a factor associated with a poor prognosis in Hodgkin's lymphoma, as identified in a 1998 NEJM paper.

title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Prognosis: Disease Stage
content: Stage IV disease is a factor associated with a poor prognosis in Hodgkin's lymphoma, as identified in a 1998 NEJM paper.

title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Prognosis: Haemoglobin Level
content: A haemoglobin level < 10.5 g/dl is a factor associated with a poor prognosis in Hodgkin's lymphoma, as identified in a 1998 NEJM paper.

title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Prognosis: Lymphocyte Count
content: A lymphocyte count < 600/µl or < 8% is a factor associated with a poor prognosis in Hodgkin's lymphoma, as identified in a 1998 NEJM paper.

title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Prognosis: Gender
content: Being male is a factor associated with a poor prognosis in Hodgkin's lymphoma, as identified in a 1998 NEJM paper.

title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Prognosis: Albumin Level
content: An albumin level < 40 g/l is a factor associated with a poor prognosis in Hodgkin's lymphoma, as identified in a 1998 NEJM paper.

title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Prognosis: White Blood Cell Count
content: A white blood count > 15,000/µl is a factor associated with a poor prognosis in Hodgkin's lymphoma, as identified in a 1998 NEJM paper.

title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Staging Imaging
content: Positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) is the mainstay of imaging for staging Hodgkin's lymphoma.

title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Ann-Arbor Staging System Overview
content: The Ann-Arbor staging system was historically the main way patients with Hodgkin's lymphoma were staged.

title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Ann-Arbor Stage I
content: Ann-Arbor Stage I involves a single lymph node.

title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Ann-Arbor Stage II
content: Ann-Arbor Stage II involves 2 or more lymph nodes/regions on the same side of the diaphragm.

title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Ann-Arbor Stage III
content: Ann-Arbor Stage III involves nodes on both sides of the diaphragm.

title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Ann-Arbor Stage IV
content: Ann-Arbor Stage IV involves spread beyond lymph nodes.

title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Ann-Arbor Subdivision A
content: Ann-Arbor staging subdivision 'A' indicates no systemic symptoms other than pruritus.

title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Ann-Arbor Subdivision B
content: Ann-Arbor staging subdivision 'B' indicates weight loss > 10% in the last 6 months, fever > 38°C, or night sweats, which signifies a poor prognosis.

title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Lugano Classification Overview
content: The Lugano classification is a system used to stage Hodgkin's lymphoma and other lymphomas, updating the Ann Arbor system by incorporating modern imaging techniques, particularly PET scans.

title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Lugano Stage I
content: Lugano Stage I involves a single lymph node region (I) or a single extralymphatic organ or site (IE).

title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Lugano Stage II
content: Lugano Stage II involves two or more lymph node regions on the same side of the diaphragm (II) or localized involvement of an extralymphatic organ or site and one or more lymph node regions on the same side of the diaphragm (IIE).

title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Lugano Stage III
content: Lugano Stage III involves lymph node regions on both sides of the diaphragm (III), which may also be accompanied by localized involvement of an extralymphatic organ or site (IIIE), involvement of the spleen (IIIS), or both (IIIE+S).

title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Lugano Stage IV
content: Lugano Stage IV involves diffuse or disseminated involvement of one or more extralymphatic organs, with or without associated lymph node involvement.

title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Lugano A/B Symptom Designation
content: In the Lugano classification, 'A' designates the absence of significant symptoms, while 'B' designates the presence of fever, night sweats, or weight loss.

title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Lugano E Designation
content: In the Lugano classification, the letter 'E' denotes the presence of extranodal disease.

title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Lugano S Designation
content: In the Lugano classification, the letter 'S' denotes involvement of the spleen.

title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Lugano X Designation
content: In the Lugano classification, the letter 'X' denotes bulky disease (large tumor mass).

title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Lugano Classification and PET Scans
content: The Lugano classification emphasizes the role of PET scans in determining the stage of Hodgkin's lymphoma, particularly in assessing metabolic activity.

title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Management Mainstay
content: Chemotherapy is the mainstay of treatment for Hodgkin's lymphoma.

title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – ABVD Chemotherapy Regimen
content: ABVD (doxorubicin, bleomycin, vinblastine, and dacarbazine) is considered the standard chemotherapy regimen for Hodgkin's lymphoma.

title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – BEACOPP Chemotherapy Regimen
content: BEACOPP (bleomycin, etoposide, doxorubicin, cyclophosphamide, vincristine, procarbazine, and prednisone) is an alternative chemotherapy regimen for Hodgkin's lymphoma with better remission rates but higher toxicity.

title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Radiotherapy
content: Radiotherapy is a treatment option for Hodgkin's lymphoma.

title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Combined Modality Therapy (CMT)
content: Combined modality therapy (CMT), involving chemotherapy followed by radiotherapy, is used in the management of Hodgkin's lymphoma.

title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Hematopoietic Cell Transplantation
content: Hematopoietic cell transplantation may be used for relapsed or refractory classic Hodgkin lymphoma.

title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Complications of Treatment (Long-term Survival)
content: Most patients with Hodgkin's lymphoma now achieve long-term survival free of the disease with modern therapy, making complications of treatment a significant concern.

title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Complications of Treatment (Secondary Malignancies)
content: Secondary malignancies, particularly solid tumors such as breast and lung cancer, are a risk associated with Hodgkin's lymphoma treatment.

title: Hyposplenism – Definition
content: Hyposplenism refers to reduced splenic function.

title: Hyposplenism – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Causes of hyposplenism include splenectomy, sickle-cell anaemia, coeliac disease, dermatitis herpetiformis, Graves' disease, systemic lupus erythematosus, and amyloidosis.

title: Hyposplenism – Clinical features
content: Blood film features of hyposplenism include Howell-Jolly bodies and siderocytes.

title: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura – Definition
content: Immune (or idiopathic) thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) is an immune-mediated reduction in the platelet count. Antibodies are directed against the glycoprotein IIb/IIIa or Ib-V-IX complex.

title: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura – Epidemiology - Adult vs. Childhood
content: Children with ITP usually have an acute thrombocytopenia that may follow infection or vaccination. In contrast, adults tend to have a more chronic condition.

title: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura – Epidemiology
content: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) is more common in older females.

title: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura – Clinical features - Incidental finding
content: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) may be detected incidentally following routine blood tests.

title: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura – Clinical features - Petechiae/Purpura
content: Symptomatic patients with Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) may present with petechiae and purpura.

title: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura – Clinical features - Bleeding
content: Symptomatic patients with Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) may present with bleeding, such as epistaxis.

title: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura – Clinical features - Catastrophic bleeding
content: Catastrophic bleeding, such as intracranial bleeding, is not a common presentation of Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP).

title: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura – Investigations - Full Blood Count
content: A full blood count in Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) typically shows isolated thrombocytopenia.

title: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura – Investigations - Bone Marrow Examination
content: A bone marrow examination is no longer routinely used in the investigation of Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP).

title: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura – Investigations - Antiplatelet Antibody Testing
content: Antiplatelet antibody testing for Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) has poor sensitivity and does not affect clinical management, so it is not commonly performed.

title: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura – Management - First-line treatment
content: The first-line treatment for Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) is oral prednisolone.

title: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura – Management - IVIG
content: Pooled normal human immunoglobulin (IVIG) may be used in Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) if active bleeding or an urgent invasive procedure is required, as it raises the platelet count quicker than steroids.

title: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura – Management - Splenectomy
content: Splenectomy is now less commonly used in the management of Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP).

title: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura – Evan's Syndrome
content: Evan's syndrome is characterized by Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) in association with autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (AIHA).

title: Iron deficiency anaemia – Definition
content: Iron deficiency anaemia is the most common anaemia worldwide. Iron is needed to make the haemoglobin in red blood cells, therefore a deficiency of iron leads to a reduction in red blood cells/haemoglobin i.e. anaemia.

title: Iron deficiency anaemia – Epidemiology
content: Globally, iron deficiency is the most common cause of anaemia. Preschool-age children have the highest prevalence of iron deficiency anaemia.

title: Iron deficiency anaemia – Serum iron
content: In Iron deficiency anaemia, serum iron is low, typically less than 8.

title: Anaemia of chronic disease – Serum iron
content: In Anaemia of chronic disease, serum iron is low, typically less than 15.

title: Iron deficiency anaemia – TIBC
content: In Iron deficiency anaemia, Total Iron Binding Capacity (TIBC) is high.

title: Anaemia of chronic disease – TIBC
content: In Anaemia of chronic disease, Total Iron Binding Capacity (TIBC) is low.

title: Iron deficiency anaemia – Transferrin saturation
content: In Iron deficiency anaemia, transferrin saturation is low.

title: Anaemia of chronic disease – Transferrin saturation
content: In Anaemia of chronic disease, transferrin saturation is low.

title: Iron deficiency anaemia – Ferritin
content: In Iron deficiency anaemia, ferritin is low.

title: Anaemia of chronic disease – Ferritin
content: In Anaemia of chronic disease, ferritin is high.

title: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura – Investigations: Antiplatelet autoantibodies
content: Antiplatelet autoantibodies (usually IgG) are investigated in Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP).

title: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura – Investigations: Bone marrow aspiration
content: Bone marrow aspiration shows megakaryocytes in the marrow in Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP). This should be carried out prior to the commencement of steroids in order to rule out leukaemia.

title: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura – Management: Oral prednisolone
content: Oral prednisolone is a first-line treatment for Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP), with 80% of patients responding.

title: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura – Management: Splenectomy
content: Splenectomy is considered for Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) if platelets are < 30 after 3 months of steroid therapy.

title: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura – Management: IV immunoglobulins
content: IV immunoglobulins can be used in the management of Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP).

title: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura – Management: Immunosuppressive drugs
content: Immunosuppressive drugs, such as cyclophosphamide, are used in the management of Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP).

title: Intravascular haemolysis – Haptoglobin decrease
content: Haptoglobin binds to free haemoglobin. A decrease in haptoglobin is an interpretation of intravascular haemolysis.

title: Hereditary spherocytosis – MCHC increased
content: Increased MCHC is a laboratory finding in hereditary spherocytosis.

title: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia – MCHC increased
content: Increased MCHC is a laboratory finding in autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, associated with spherocytosis.

title: Microcytic anaemia – MCHC decreased
content: Decreased MCHC is a laboratory finding in microcytic anaemia (e.g., iron deficiency).

title: Lead poisoning – Definition
content: Lead poisoning is the result of lead, a heavy metal, building up in the body, often over months or years. Even small amounts of lead can cause serious health problems.

title: Lead poisoning – Vulnerable populations
content: Children younger than age 6 are especially vulnerable to lead poisoning, which can severely affect how a child's body grows and brain develops.

title: Lead poisoning – Common sources in children
content: Lead-based paint and lead-contaminated dust in older buildings are common sources of lead poisoning in children. Other sources include contaminated air, water and soil.

title: Lead poisoning – Occupational exposure
content: Adults who work with batteries, do home renovations or work in auto repair shops might be exposed to lead.

title: Lead poisoning – Cause: Lead in paint
content: Lead-based paints for homes, children's toys and household furniture have been banned in the United States since 1978. Most lead poisoning in children results from eating chips of deteriorating lead-based paint.

title: Lead poisoning – Cause: Water pipes and canned goods
content: Lead pipes, brass plumbing fixtures and copper pipes soldered with lead can release lead particles into tap water. Lead solder in food cans, banned in the United States, is still used in some countries.

title: Lead poisoning – Cause: Soil contamination
content: Lead particles from leaded gasoline or paint settle on soil and can last years. Lead-contaminated soil is still a major problem around highways and in some urban settings.

title: Lead poisoning – Cause: Household dust
content: Household dust can contain lead from lead paint chips or from contaminated soil brought in from outside.

title: Lead poisoning – Cause: Pottery
content: Glazes found on some ceramics, china and porcelain can contain lead that can leach into food served or stored in the pottery.

title: Lead poisoning – Cause: Toys
content: Lead is sometimes found in toys and other products produced abroad.

title: Lead poisoning – Cause: Cosmetics
content: Tiro, an eye cosmetic from Nigeria, has been linked to lead poisoning. Kohl is another eye makeup that may contain lead.

title: Lead poisoning – Cause: Herbal or folk remedies
content: Lead poisoning has been linked to greta and azarcon, traditional Hispanic medicines, as well as some from India, China and other countries.

title: Lead poisoning – Cause: Tamarind candy
content: Some candies made with the tropical fruit tamarind have been found to contain lead, possibly due to how the candy was processed or stored.

title: Lead poisoning – Cause: Lead bullets
content: Time spent at firing ranges can lead to exposure to lead.

title: Lead poisoning – Cause: Occupations
content: People are exposed to lead and can bring it home on their clothes when they work in auto repair, mining, pipe fitting, battery manufacturing, painting, construction and certain other fields.

title: Lead poisoning – Risk factor: Age
content: Infants and young children are more likely to be exposed to lead than are older children. They might chew paint that flakes off walls and woodwork, and their hands can be contaminated with lead dust. Young children also absorb lead more easily, and it's more harmful for them than it is for adults and older children.

title: Lead poisoning – Risk factor: Living in an older home
content: Although the use of lead-based paints has been banned since the 1970s, older homes and buildings often retain remnants of this paint. People renovating an older home are at even higher risk.

title: Lead poisoning – Risk factor: Certain hobbies
content: Making stained glass and some jewelry requires the use of lead solder. Refinishing old furniture might put you in contact with layers of lead paint.

title: Lead poisoning – Risk factor: Living in developing countries
content: Developing countries often have less strict rules regarding exposure to lead than do developed countries. American families who adopt a child from another country might want to have the child's blood tested for lead poisoning.

title: Lead poisoning – Risk factor: Pregnancy
content: Lead can harm an unborn child. If you're pregnant or planning a pregnancy, be especially careful to avoid exposure to lead.

title: Lead poisoning – Clinical features in children: Developmental delay
content: Signs and symptoms of lead poisoning in children include developmental delay.

title: Lead poisoning – Clinical features in children: Learning difficulties
content: Signs and symptoms of lead poisoning in children include learning difficulties.

title: Lead poisoning – Clinical features in children: Irritability
content: Signs and symptoms of lead poisoning in children include irritability.

title: Lead poisoning – Clinical features in children: Loss of appetite
content: Signs and symptoms of lead poisoning in children include loss of appetite.

title: Lead poisoning – Clinical features in children: Weight loss
content: Signs and symptoms of lead poisoning in children include weight loss.

title: Lead poisoning – Clinical features in children: Sluggishness and fatigue
content: Signs and symptoms of lead poisoning in children include sluggishness and fatigue.

title: Lead poisoning – Clinical features in children: Abdominal pain
content: Signs and symptoms of lead poisoning in children include abdominal pain.

title: Lead poisoning – Clinical features in children: Vomiting
content: Signs and symptoms of lead poisoning in children include vomiting.

title: Lead poisoning – Clinical features in children: Constipation
content: Signs and symptoms of lead poisoning in children include constipation.

title: Lead poisoning – Clinical features in children: Hearing loss
content: Signs and symptoms of lead poisoning in children include hearing loss.

title: Lead poisoning – Clinical features in children: Seizures
content: Signs and symptoms of lead poisoning in children include seizures.

title: Lead poisoning – Clinical features in newborns: Premature birth
content: Babies exposed to lead before birth might be born early.

title: Lead poisoning – Clinical features in newborns: Low birth weight
content: Babies exposed to lead before birth might have lower birth weight.

title: Lead poisoning – Clinical features in newborns: Slowed growth
content: Babies exposed to lead before birth might have slowed growth.

title: Lead poisoning – Clinical features in adults: High blood pressure
content: Signs and symptoms of lead poisoning in adults might include high blood pressure.

title: Lead poisoning – Clinical features in adults: Joint and muscle pain
content: Signs and symptoms of lead poisoning in adults might include joint and muscle pain.

title: Lead poisoning – Clinical features in adults: Difficulties with memory or concentration
content: Signs and symptoms of lead poisoning in adults might include difficulties with memory or concentration.

title: Lead poisoning – Clinical features in adults: Headache
content: Signs and symptoms of lead poisoning in adults might include headache.

title: Lead poisoning – Clinical features in adults: Abdominal pain
content: Signs and symptoms of lead poisoning in adults might include abdominal pain.

title: Lead poisoning – Clinical features in adults: Mood disorders
content: Signs and symptoms of lead poisoning in adults might include mood disorders.

title: Lead poisoning – Clinical features in adults: Reduced sperm count and abnormal sperm
content: Signs and symptoms of lead poisoning in adults might include reduced sperm count and abnormal sperm.

title: Lead poisoning – Clinical features in adults: Miscarriage, stillbirth or premature birth
content: Signs and symptoms of lead poisoning in adults might include miscarriage, stillbirth or premature birth.

title: Lead poisoning – Investigation: Blood test
content: A blood test can be used to check the blood lead level.

title: Lead poisoning – Investigation: Basophilic stippling
content: Basophilic stippling on a blood film is associated with lead poisoning.

title: Lead poisoning – Complication: Brain development damage in children
content: The greatest risk of lead poisoning in children is to brain development, where damage that can't be reversed can happen.

title: Lead poisoning – Complication: Kidney and nervous system damage
content: High lead levels can damage the kidneys and nervous system in both children and adults.

title: Lead poisoning – Complication: Seizures, unconsciousness and death
content: Very high lead levels may cause seizures, unconsciousness and death.

title: Lead poisoning – Prevention: Wash hands and toys
content: To help reduce hand-to-mouth transfer of contaminated dust or soil, wash children's hands after outdoor play, before eating and at bedtime. Wash their toys regularly.

title: Lead poisoning – Prevention: Clean dusty surfaces
content: Clean floors with a wet mop and wipe furniture, windowsills and other dusty surfaces with a damp cloth.

title: Lead poisoning – Prevention: Remove shoes before entering the house
content: Remove shoes before entering the house to help keep lead-based soil outside.

title: Lead poisoning – Prevention: Run cold water
content: If you have older plumbing containing lead pipes or fittings, run your cold water for at least a minute before using. Don't use hot tap water to make baby formula or for cooking.

title: Lead poisoning – Prevention: Keep children from playing on soil
content: Provide children with a sandbox that's covered when not in use. Plant grass or cover bare soil with mulch.

title: Lead poisoning – Prevention: Choose healthy foods
content: Regular meals and good nutrition might help lower lead absorption. Children especially need enough calcium, vitamin C and iron in their diets to help keep lead from being absorbed.

title: Lead poisoning – Prevention: Maintain painted surfaces in your home
content: If your home has lead-based paint, check regularly for peeling paint and fix problems promptly. Try not to sand, which generates dust particles that contain lead.

title: Lymphadenopathy – Definition
content: Lymphadenopathy refers to the condition of enlarged lymph nodes, typically indicating an immune response to an infection or malignancy. Understanding its underlying causes and appropriate management is crucial in patient care.

title: Lymphadenopathy – Background: Lymphatic System Function
content: The lymphatic system, comprising lymph vessels, nodes, and other tissues, plays a critical role in body's immunity. Lymph nodes are small, bean-shaped structures that produce and store cells that fight infection and disease. They filter the lymph fluid as it flows through them, trapping bacteria, viruses, and other foreign substances to be destroyed by white blood cells.

title: Lymphadenopathy – Background: Mechanism of Enlargement
content: Lymphadenopathy usually occurs when lymph nodes produce more cells or become filled with debris from a destroyed cell.

title: Lymphadenopathy – Infective Causes: Infectious Mononucleosis
content: Infectious mononucleosis can cause lymphadenopathy.

title: Lymphadenopathy – Infective Causes: HIV
content: HIV, including seroconversion illness, can cause lymphadenopathy.

title: Lymphadenopathy – Infective Causes: Eczema with Secondary Infection
content: Eczema with secondary infection can cause lymphadenopathy.

title: Lymphadenopathy – Infective Causes: Rubella
content: Rubella can cause lymphadenopathy.

title: Lymphadenopathy – Infective Causes: Toxoplasmosis
content: Toxoplasmosis can cause lymphadenopathy.

title: Lymphadenopathy – Infective Causes: CMV
content: CMV can cause lymphadenopathy.

title: Lymphadenopathy – Infective Causes: Tuberculosis
content: Tuberculosis can cause lymphadenopathy.

title: Lymphadenopathy – Infective Causes: Roseola Infantum
content: Roseola infantum can cause lymphadenopathy.

title: Lymphadenopathy – Neoplastic Causes: Leukaemia
content: Leukaemia can cause lymphadenopathy.

title: Lymphadenopathy – Neoplastic Causes: Lymphoma
content: Lymphoma can cause lymphadenopathy.

title: Lymphadenopathy – Other Causes: Autoimmune Conditions
content: Autoimmune conditions such as SLE and rheumatoid arthritis can cause lymphadenopathy.

title: Lymphadenopathy – Other Causes: Graft Versus Host Disease
content: Graft versus host disease can cause lymphadenopathy.

title: Lymphadenopathy – Other Causes: Sarcoidosis
content: Sarcoidosis can cause lymphadenopathy.

title: Lymphadenopathy – Other Causes: Drugs
content: Drugs such as phenytoin, allopurinol, and isoniazid can cause lymphadenopathy.

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Clinical Features: Lymphadenopathy
content: Lymphadenopathy is a clinical feature of Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, presenting as a persistent or progressive, painless, firm, rubbery lymph node.

title: Castleman's disease – Clinical Features: Lymphadenopathy
content: Painless lymph node enlargement can occur in any lymph node group, commonly in the neck, axillae, or inguinal areas, with nodes being firm and non-tender on examination.

title: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia – Clinical Features: Lymphadenopathy
content: Lymphadenopathy is a common feature of Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, often presenting as painless enlargement of peripheral lymph nodes which are usually symmetrical and non-tender.

title: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia – Rai Staging: Stage I
content: Rai stage I of Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia is characterized by lymphadenopathy and has an overall survival of 7 years.

title: Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma – Clinical Features: Lymphadenopathy
content: In Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, lymphadenopathy can occur anywhere in the body, including the groin and abdomen.

title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Clinical Features: Lymphadenopathy
content: In Hodgkin's lymphoma, lymphadenopathy is usually limited to the upper body (neck, chest, or axilla) and can experience alcohol-induced pain in the node.

title: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome – Clinical Features: Lymphadenopathy
content: Lymphadenopathy is a clinical feature of Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome.

title: Waldenstrom's macroglobulinaemia – Clinical Features: Lymphadenopathy
content: Painless lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly may be found on physical examination in Waldenstrom's macroglobulinaemia, due to infiltration of the disease into lymphoid tissues.

title: Suspected Haematological Malignancy in Young People – Clinical Features: Generalised Lymphadenopathy
content: Generalised lymphadenopathy in a person aged 0-24 years should prompt a very urgent full blood count (within 48 hours) to investigate for leukaemia.

title: Macrocytic anaemia – Definition
content: Macrocytic anaemia can be divided into causes associated with a megaloblastic bone marrow and those with a normoblastic bone marrow.

title: Macrocytic anaemia – Megaloblastic Aetiology
content: Megaloblastic causes of macrocytic anaemia include vitamin B12 deficiency and folate deficiency (e.g., secondary to methotrexate).

title: Macrocytic anaemia – Normoblastic Aetiology
content: Normoblastic causes of macrocytic anaemia include alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism, pregnancy, reticulocytosis, myelodysplasia, and cytotoxic drugs.

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Management
content: Any of the following features in a person aged 0-24 years should prompt a very urgent full blood count (within 48 hours) to investigate for leukaemia: Pallor

title: Methaemoglobinaemia – Definition and Pathophysiology
content: Methaemoglobinaemia describes haemoglobin which has been oxidised from Fe2+ to Fe3+. This is normally regulated by NADH methaemoglobin reductase, which transfers electrons from NADH to methaemoglobin resulting in the reduction of methaemoglobin to haemoglobin. There is tissue hypoxia as Fe3+ cannot bind oxygen, and hence the oxidation dissociation curve is moved to the left.

title: Methaemoglobinaemia – Congenital Aetiology
content: Congenital causes of methaemoglobinaemia include haemoglobin chain variants (HbM, HbH) and NADH methaemoglobin reductase deficiency.

title: Methaemoglobinaemia – Association with G6PD Deficiency
content: Some variants of G6PD deficiency have been associated with methaemoglobinaemia, leading to cyanosis and dyspnoea.

title: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance – Definition
content: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS), also known as benign paraproteinaemia and monoclonal gammopathy, is a common condition that causes a paraproteinaemia and is often mistaken for myeloma.

title: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance – Prognosis
content: Around 10% of patients with MGUS eventually develop myeloma at 10 years, with 50% at 15 years.

title: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance – Non-IgM MGUS
content: Non-IgM MGUS is the most common subtype and may progress to multiple myeloma or AL amyloidosis.

title: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance – IgM MGUS
content: IgM MGUS may progress to Waldenström macroglobulinaemia or lymphoma.

title: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance – Light chain MGUS
content: Light chain MGUS has an increased risk of renal disease or AL amyloidosis.

title: Myelodysplastic syndrome – Definition
content: Myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) are a heterogeneous group of clonal hematopoietic stem cell disorders characterized by ineffective hematopoiesis, peripheral blood cytopenias, and a risk of progression to acute myeloid leukaemia (AML).

title: Myelodysplastic syndrome – Epidemiology
content: Myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) predominantly affect older adults, with a median age at diagnosis of 70-75 years.

title: Myelodysplastic syndrome – Aetiology
content: Myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) arise from genetic mutations in hematopoietic stem cells.

title: Myelodysplastic syndrome – Risk factors
content: Around 90% of Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) cases are primary, with the remaining 10% secondary to causes such as chemotherapy and radiotherapy. Secondary MDS typically develops around 5 years post-treatment.

title: Myelodysplastic syndrome – Pathophysiology
content: The key pathophysiological feature of Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) is ineffective hematopoiesis leading to peripheral cytopenias despite a typically hypercellular bone marrow.

title: Myelodysplastic syndrome – Clinical features: Anaemia
content: Common presentations of Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) include fatigue, weakness, and pallor due to anaemia.

title: Myelodysplastic syndrome – Clinical features: Neutropenia
content: Common presentations of Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) include recurrent infections due to neutropenia.

title: Myelodysplastic syndrome – Clinical features: Thrombocytopenia
content: Common presentations of Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) include easy bruising or bleeding due to thrombocytopenia.

title: Myelodysplastic syndrome – Clinical features: Asymptomatic
content: Some patients with Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) may be asymptomatic and are diagnosed incidentally on routine blood counts.

title: Myelodysplastic syndrome – Diagnosis: Overview
content: The diagnosis of Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) is based on peripheral blood counts, bone marrow examination, and cytogenetic analysis.

title: Myelodysplastic syndrome – Diagnosis: Bone marrow biopsy
content: Bone marrow biopsy in Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) typically shows dysplastic changes in hematopoietic cells and a varying degree of blasts.

title: Myelodysplastic syndrome – Diagnosis: Cytogenetic analysis
content: Cytogenetic analysis in Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) can identify specific chromosomal abnormalities that may have prognostic implications.

title: Myelodysplastic syndrome – Management: Overview
content: Treatment of Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) depends on the subtype of MDS, the patient's age and overall health, and the severity of symptoms.

title: Myelodysplastic syndrome – Management: Supportive care
content: Management options for Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) include supportive care, such as blood transfusions and growth factors.

title: Myelodysplastic syndrome – Management: Disease-modifying therapy
content: Management options for Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) include disease-modifying therapy, such as hypomethylating agents and lenalidomide.

title: Myelodysplastic syndrome – Management: Immunosuppressive therapy
content: Management options for Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) include immunosuppressive therapy.

title: Myelodysplastic syndrome – Management: Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation
content: Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is the only potentially curative option for Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS), but it is limited by the patient's age and comorbidities.

title: Myelofibrosis – Definition
content: Myelofibrosis is a rare haematologic myeloproliferative disorder characterized by the replacement of bone marrow with collagen and fibrosis. It results in haematological abnormalities, profound fatigue, massive splenomegaly, and extramedullary haematopoiesis. The disease may transform into acute myeloid leukaemia.

title: Myelofibrosis – Pathophysiology
content: Myelofibrosis is thought to be caused by hyperplasia of abnormal megakaryocytes. The resultant release of platelet-derived growth factor is believed to stimulate fibroblasts, leading to bone marrow fibrosis. Haematopoiesis develops in the liver and spleen (extramedullary haematopoiesis).

title: Myelofibrosis – Epidemiology
content: Myelofibrosis has an incidence of 0.40 cases per 100,000 person-years. It typically affects older adults, with a peak incidence between 60-70 years. The sex ratio is 1:1. The median survival is 6 years.

title: Myelofibrosis – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Myelofibrosis typically manifests in the 50 and older age group, though cases have been reported in children. There is a familial relationship and a preponderance in Ashkenazi Jews. Genes implicated include JAK2, MPL, and CALR.

title: Myelofibrosis – Clinical features: Anaemia
content: Myelofibrosis can present with symptoms of anaemia, such as fatigue, which is the most common presenting symptom, and pallor.

title: Myelofibrosis – Clinical features: Splenomegaly
content: Patients with Myelofibrosis often present with massive splenomegaly.

title: Myelofibrosis – Clinical features: Hypermetabolic symptoms
content: Hypermetabolic symptoms in Myelofibrosis include weight loss and night sweats.

title: Myelofibrosis – Laboratory findings: Anaemia
content: Laboratory findings in Myelofibrosis include anaemia.

title: Myelofibrosis – Laboratory findings: White blood cell and platelet count
content: Early in the disease, Myelofibrosis may show high white blood cell (WBC) and platelet counts.

title: Myelofibrosis – Laboratory findings: Blood film
content: A blood film in Myelofibrosis typically shows 'tear-drop' poikilocytes and multiple forms of immature red cells.

title: Myelofibrosis – Laboratory findings: Bone marrow biopsy
content: Bone marrow aspirate in Myelofibrosis is usually a 'dry tap', meaning it is unobtainable. A trephine biopsy is therefore needed to demonstrate marked fibrosis.

title: Myelofibrosis – Laboratory findings: Urate and LDH
content: Myelofibrosis is associated with high urate and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) levels, reflecting increased cell turnover.

title: Neutropenia – Definition
content: Neutropenia is characterized by low functional neutrophils, which can occur even if total white cell counts are high, leading to recurrent or severe infections.

title: Neutropenia – Severe Neutropenia Definition
content: Severe neutropenia is defined as an absolute neutrophil count of <500 cells/µL, which is associated with a high risk of infections.

title: Neutropenia – Clinical Features
content: Neutropenia leads to recurrent or severe infections.

title: Neutropenia – Management
content: Patients with neutropenia may require antibiotic prophylaxis.

title: Acute Myeloid Leukaemia – Clinical Features
content: In Acute Myeloid Leukaemia, neutropenia can lead to recurrent or severe infections.

title: Myelodysplastic Syndrome – Clinical Features
content: Recurrent infections due to neutropenia are common presentations of Myelodysplastic Syndrome.

title: Acute Lymphoblastic Leukaemia – Pathophysiology
content: In Acute Lymphoblastic Leukaemia, abnormal lymphoblasts alter the bone marrow niche, leading to cytopenias such as neutropenia, which causes associated clinical symptoms like infections.

title: Chronic Lymphocytic Leukaemia – Clinical Features
content: In Chronic Lymphocytic Leukaemia, bone marrow infiltration can lead to neutropenia, resulting in susceptibility to infections.

title: Chemotherapy – Complications
content: Myelosuppression, a common complication of chemotherapy, leads to neutropenia, increasing susceptibility to infections.

title: Neutropenic sepsis – Definition
content: Neutropenic sepsis is a relatively common complication of cancer therapy, usually as a consequence of chemotherapy. It most commonly occurs 7-14 days after chemotherapy. It may be defined as a neutrophil count of < 0.5 * 109 in a patient who is having anticancer treatment and has one of the following: a temperature higher than 38ºC or other signs or symptoms consistent with clinically significant sepsis

title: Neutropenic sepsis – Aetiology
content: coagulase-negative, Gram-positive bacteria are the most common cause, particularly Staphylococcus epidermidis. this is probably due to the use of indwelling lines in patients with cancer

title: Neutropenic sepsis – Prophylaxis
content: if it is anticipated that patients are likely to have a neutrophil count of < 0.5 * 109 as a consequence of their treatment they should be offered a fluoroquinolone

title: Neutropenic sepsis – Initial empirical antibiotic therapy
content: antibiotics must be started immediately, do not wait for the WBC. NICE recommends starting empirical antibiotic therapy with piperacillin with tazobactam (Tazocin) immediately

title: Neutropenic sepsis – Vancomycin in central venous access
content: many units add vancomycin if the patient has central venous access but NICE do not support this approach

title: Neutropenic sepsis – Outpatient assessment and risk stratification
content: following this initial treatment patients are usually assessed by a specialist and risk-stratified to see if they may be able to have outpatient treatment

title: Neutropenic sepsis – Alternative antibiotics for non-response
content: if patients are still febrile and unwell after 48 hours an alternative antibiotic such as meropenem is often prescribed +/- vancomycin

title: Neutropenic sepsis – Investigations for fungal infections
content: if patients are not responding after 4-6 days the Christie guidelines suggest ordering investigations for fungal infections (e.g. HRCT), rather than just starting therapy antifungal therapy blindly

title: Neutropenic sepsis – Role of G-CSF
content: there may be a role for G-CSF in selected patients

title: Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma – Definition
content: Lymphoma is the malignant proliferation of lymphocytes which accumulate in lymph nodes or other organs. Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma is every type of lymphoma that is not Hodgkin's lymphoma. Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma may affect either B or T-cells and can be further classified as high grade or low grade.

title: Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma – Epidemiology
content: Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma is the 6th most common cause of cancer in the UK.

title: Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma – Risk factors
content: Elderly age is a risk factor for Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma.

title: Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma – Clinical features
content: Painless lymphadenopathy (non-tender, rubbery, asymmetrical) is a symptom of Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma.

title: Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma – Investigations
content: Excisional node biopsy is the diagnostic investigation of choice for Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma.

title: Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma – Staging
content: Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma is staged using the Lugano staging system.

title: Normocytic anaemia – Anaemia of chronic disease
content: Anaemia of chronic disease is a cause of normocytic anaemia.

title: Normocytic anaemia – Chronic kidney disease
content: Chronic kidney disease is a cause of normocytic anaemia.

title: Normocytic anaemia – Aplastic anaemia
content: Aplastic anaemia is a cause of normocytic anaemia.

title: Normocytic anaemia – Haemolytic anaemia
content: Haemolytic anaemia is a cause of normocytic anaemia.

title: Normocytic anaemia – Acute blood loss
content: Acute blood loss is a cause of normocytic anaemia.

title: Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria – Definition
content: Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria (PNH) is an acquired disorder leading to haemolysis (mainly intravascular) of haematological cells. It is thought to be caused by increased sensitivity of cell membranes to complement due to a lack of glycoprotein glycosyl-phosphatidylinositol (GPI).

title: Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria is thought to be caused by increased sensitivity of cell membranes to complement due to a lack of glycoprotein glycosyl-phosphatidylinositol (GPI).

title: Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria – Clinical features
content: Patients are more prone to venous thrombosis.

title: Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria – Pathophysiology
content: GPI can be thought of as an anchor which attaches surface proteins to the cell membrane.

title: Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria – Complications
content: Aplastic anaemia may develop in some patients with Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria.

title: Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria – Investigations
content: Flow cytometry of blood to detect low levels of CD59 and CD55 has now replaced Ham's test as the gold standard investigation in PNH.

title: Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria – Management
content: Blood product replacement is a management strategy for Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria.

title: Platelet transfusion – Indication (Active Bleeding)
content: Platelet transfusion may be used if active bleeding or an urgent invasive procedure is required, as it raises the platelet count quicker than steroids.

title: Platelet transfusion – Emergency Management (Severe Bleeding)
content: For emergency situations involving severe bleeding or critically low platelet counts, immediate intervention includes high-dose IVIg and/or platelet transfusions.

title: Polycythaemia – Definition and Classification
content: Polycythaemia is a condition that may be classified as relative, primary (polycythaemia rubra vera), or secondary.

title: Polycythaemia – Relative Causes
content: Relative causes of polycythaemia include dehydration and stress (Gaisbock syndrome).

title: Polycythaemia – Primary Cause
content: The primary cause of polycythaemia is polycythaemia rubra vera.

title: Polycythaemia – Secondary Causes
content: Secondary causes of polycythaemia include COPD, altitude, obstructive sleep apnoea, and excessive erythropoietin production due to conditions such as cerebellar haemangioma, hypernephroma, hepatoma, and uterine fibroids.

title: Polycythaemia – Red Cell Mass Studies
content: Red cell mass studies are used to differentiate between true (primary or secondary) polycythaemia and relative polycythaemia. In true polycythaemia, the total red cell mass is > 35 ml/kg in males and > 32 ml/kg in women.

title: Polycythaemia vera – Definition
content: Polycythaemia vera is a myeloproliferative disorder caused by clonal proliferation of a marrow stem cell leading to an increase in red cell volume, often accompanied by overproduction of neutrophils and platelets.

title: Polycythaemia vera – Genetics
content: A mutation in JAK2 is present in approximately 95% of patients with polycythaemia vera.

title: Polycythaemia vera – Epidemiology
content: The incidence of polycythaemia vera peaks in the sixth decade.

title: Polycythaemia vera – Clinical features
content: Pruritus, typically after a hot bath, is a feature of Polycythaemia vera.

title: Polycythaemia vera – Investigations
content: The British Committee for Standards in Haematology (BCSH) recommends a full blood count/film, which may show raised haematocrit; neutrophils, basophils, and platelets raised in half of patients.

title: Polycythaemia vera – Investigations (JAK2 negative)
content: If JAK2 mutation is negative and there are no obvious secondary causes, the BCSH suggests red cell mass testing.

title: Polycythaemia vera – Other features
content: A raised leukocyte alkaline phosphatase may be seen in Polycythaemia vera.

title: Polycythaemia vera – Diagnostic Criteria (JAK2-positive)
content: For JAK2-positive polycythaemia vera, diagnosis requires high haematocrit (>0.52 in men, >0.48 in women) OR raised red cell mass (>25% above predicted).

title: Polycythaemia vera – Diagnostic Criteria (JAK2-negative)
content: For JAK2-negative PRV, diagnosis requires raised red cell mass (>25% above predicted) OR haematocrit >0.60 in men, >0.56 in women.

title: Polycythaemia vera – Management - Aspirin
content: Aspirin reduces the risk of thrombotic events in Polycythaemia vera.

title: Polycythaemia vera – Management - Venesection
content: Venesection is the first-line treatment to keep the haemoglobin in the normal range for Polycythaemia vera.

title: Polycythaemia vera – Management - Chemotherapy (Hydroxyurea)
content: Hydroxyurea is a chemotherapy option for Polycythaemia vera, with a slight increased risk of secondary leukaemia.

title: Polycythaemia vera – Management - Chemotherapy (Phosphorus-32)
content: Phosphorus-32 therapy is a chemotherapy option for Polycythaemia vera.

title: Polycythaemia vera – Prognosis - Thrombotic events
content: Thrombotic events are a significant cause of morbidity and mortality in Polycythaemia vera.

title: Polycythaemia vera – Prognosis - Progression to myelofibrosis
content: 5-15% of patients with Polycythaemia vera progress to myelofibrosis.

title: Polycythaemia vera – Prognosis - Progression to acute leukaemia
content: 5-15% of patients with Polycythaemia vera progress to acute leukaemia (risk increased with chemotherapy treatment).

title: Post-thrombotic syndrome – Definition
content: Post-thrombotic syndrome is a clinical syndrome that patients may develop following a DVT, resulting from venous outflow obstruction and venous insufficiency leading to chronic venous hypertension.

title: Post-thrombotic syndrome – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Post-thrombotic syndrome develops following a Deep vein thrombosis (DVT).

title: Post-thrombotic syndrome – Pathophysiology
content: Venous outflow obstruction and venous insufficiency lead to chronic venous hypertension in post-thrombotic syndrome.

title: Post-thrombotic syndrome – Clinical features
content: Patients with post-thrombotic syndrome may experience painful, heavy calves.

title: Post-thrombotic syndrome – Management
content: Compression stockings are not recommended to reduce the risk of post-thrombotic syndrome following a deep vein thrombosis.

title: Venous thromboembolism - Pregnancy as a risk factor
content: Pregnancy is a common predisposing factor for venous thromboembolism (VTE).

title: Venous thromboembolism - Puerperium as a risk factor
content: The puerperium period is a common predisposing factor for venous thromboembolism (VTE).

title: Primary immunodeficiency – Classification
content: Primary immunodeficiency disorders are classified according to which component of the immune system they affect.

title: Primary immunodeficiency – Chronic granulomatous disease: Underlying defect
content: Chronic granulomatous disease is caused by a lack of NADPH oxidase, which reduces the ability of phagocytes to produce reactive oxygen species.

title: Primary immunodeficiency – Chronic granulomatous disease: Clinical features
content: Chronic granulomatous disease causes recurrent pneumonias and abscesses, particularly due to catalase-positive bacteria (e.g. Staphylococcus aureus) and fungi (e.g. Aspergillus).

title: Primary immunodeficiency – Chronic granulomatous disease: Investigations
content: Chronic granulomatous disease is diagnosed by a negative nitroblue-tetrazolium test and an abnormal dihydrorhodamine flow cytometry test.

title: Primary immunodeficiency – Chediak-Higashi syndrome: Underlying defect
content: Chediak-Higashi syndrome is caused by a defect in lysosomal trafficking regulator protein.

title: Primary immunodeficiency – Chediak-Higashi syndrome: Clinical features
content: Chediak-Higashi syndrome is characterized by giant granules in neutrophils and platelets.

title: Primary immunodeficiency – Leukocyte adhesion deficiency: Underlying defect
content: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency is caused by a defect of LFA-1 integrin (CD18) protein on neutrophils.

title: Primary immunodeficiency – Leukocyte adhesion deficiency: Clinical features
content: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency presents with recurrent bacterial infections, delay in umbilical cord sloughing, and absence of neutrophils/pus at sites of infection.

title: Primary immunodeficiency – Common variable immunodeficiency: Underlying defect
content: Common variable immunodeficiency has many varying causes, leading to low antibody levels, specifically in immunoglobulin (Ig) types IgG, IgM and IgA.

title: Primary immunodeficiency – Common variable immunodeficiency: Clinical features
content: Common variable immunodeficiency presents with recurrent chest infections and may predispose to autoimmune disorders and lymphoma.

title: Primary immunodeficiency – Bruton's (x-linked) congenital agammaglobulinaemia: Underlying defect
content: Bruton's (x-linked) congenital agammaglobulinaemia is an X-linked recessive condition caused by a defect in the Bruton's tyrosine kinase (BTK) gene, leading to a severe block in B cell development.

title: Primary immunodeficiency – Bruton's (x-linked) congenital agammaglobulinaemia: Clinical features
content: Bruton's (x-linked) congenital agammaglobulinaemia presents with recurrent bacterial infections and absence of B-cells with reduced immunoglobulins of all classes.

title: Primary immunodeficiency – Selective immunoglobulin A deficiency: Underlying defect
content: Selective immunoglobulin A deficiency is caused by a maturation defect in B cells.

title: Primary immunodeficiency – Selective immunoglobulin A deficiency: Clinical features
content: Selective immunoglobulin A deficiency is the most common primary antibody deficiency, presenting with recurrent sinus and respiratory infections. It is associated with coeliac disease and may cause false negative coeliac antibody screens. Severe reactions to blood transfusions may occur (anti-IgA antibodies → anaphylaxis).

title: Primary immunodeficiency – DiGeorge syndrome: Underlying defect
content: DiGeorge syndrome is caused by a 22q11.2 deletion, leading to failure to develop the 3rd and 4th pharyngeal pouches.

title: Primary immunodeficiency – DiGeorge syndrome: Clinical features
content: Common features of DiGeorge syndrome include congenital heart disease (e.g. tetralogy of Fallot), learning difficulties, hypocalcaemia, recurrent viral/fungal diseases, and cleft palate.

title: Primary immunodeficiency – Severe combined immunodeficiency: Underlying defect
content: Severe combined immunodeficiency has many varying causes; the most common (X-linked) is due to a defect in the common gamma chain, a protein used in the receptors for IL-2 and other interleukins. Other causes include adenosine deaminase deficiency.

title: Primary immunodeficiency – Severe combined immunodeficiency: Clinical features
content: Severe combined immunodeficiency presents with recurrent infections due to viruses, bacteria, and fungi, and reduced T-cell receptor excision circles. Stem cell transplantation may be successful.

title: Primary immunodeficiency – Ataxic telangiectasia: Underlying defect
content: Ataxic telangiectasia is an autosomal recessive condition caused by a defect in DNA repair enzymes.

title: Primary immunodeficiency – Ataxic telangiectasia: Clinical features
content: Ataxic telangiectasia features include cerebellar ataxia, telangiectasia (spider angiomas), recurrent chest infections, and a 10% risk of developing malignancy, lymphoma or leukaemia.

title: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome – Underlying defect
content: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome is inherited in an X-linked recessive fashion and is caused by a mutation in the WASP gene.

title: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome – Clinical features
content: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome causes primary immunodeficiency due to combined B- and T-cell dysfunction. Features include recurrent bacterial infections (e.g. chest), eczema, thrombocytopaenia, and low IgM levels. There is an increased risk of autoimmune disorders and malignancy.

title: Primary immunodeficiency – Hyper IgM Syndromes: Underlying defect
content: Hyper IgM Syndromes are caused by mutations in the CD40 gene.

title: Primary immunodeficiency – Hyper IgM Syndromes: Clinical features
content: Hyper IgM Syndromes present with infection/Pneumocystis pneumonia, hepatitis, and diarrhoea.

title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Definition
content: Sickle-cell anaemia is an autosomal recessive condition that results from the synthesis of an abnormal haemoglobin chain termed HbS.

title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Epidemiology
content: Sickle-cell anaemia is more common in people of African descent as the heterozygous condition offers some protection against malaria.

title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Clinical features
content: Symptoms in homozygotes don't tend to develop until 4-6 months when the abnormal HbSS molecules take over from fetal haemoglobin.

title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Pathophysiology
content: Normal haemoglobin is designated as HbAA.

title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Investigations
content: The definitive diagnosis of sickle cell disease is by haemoglobin electrophoresis.

title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Management
content: Crisis management for sickle-cell anaemia includes analgesia (e.g., opiates), rehydration, and oxygen.

title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Crises types
content: Recognised types of sickle-cell crises include thrombotic (vaso-occlusive/painful crises), acute chest syndrome, anaemic, aplastic, sequestration, and infection.

title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Thrombotic crises
content: Thrombotic crises, also known as painful crises or vaso-occlusive crises, are precipitated by infection, dehydration, or deoxygenation (e.g., high altitude).

title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Acute chest syndrome
content: Acute chest syndrome is caused by vaso-occlusion within the pulmonary microvasculature, leading to infarction in the lung parenchyma.

title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Acute chest syndrome management
content: Management of acute chest syndrome includes pain relief, respiratory support (e.g., oxygen therapy), antibiotics, transfusion to improve oxygenation, and incentive spirometry to reduce atelectasis and improve alveolar ventilation.

title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Aplastic crises
content: Aplastic crises are caused by infection with parvovirus, leading to a sudden fall in haemoglobin and bone marrow suppression with a reduced reticulocyte count.

title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Sequestration crises
content: Sequestration crises involve sickling within organs such as the spleen or lungs, causing pooling of blood with worsening of anaemia and an increased reticulocyte count.

title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Complications
content: The majority of adult patients with sickle-cell will have an atrophied spleen due to repeated infarction.

title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Risk factors for VTE
content: Sickle cell disease is an underlying condition that increases the risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE).

title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Management - Crisis management: Analgesia
content: Analgesia, e.g., opiates, is used in the crisis management of sickle-cell anaemia.

title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Management - Crisis management: Rehydration
content: Rehydration is used in the crisis management of sickle-cell anaemia.

title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Management - Crisis management: Oxygen
content: Oxygen is used in the crisis management of sickle-cell anaemia.

title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Management - Crisis management: Antibiotics
content: Antibiotics should be considered in the crisis management of sickle-cell anaemia if there is evidence of infection.

title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Management - Crisis management: Blood transfusion
content: Blood transfusion is used in the crisis management of sickle-cell anaemia.

title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Management - Crisis management: Exchange transfusion
content: Exchange transfusion is used in the crisis management of sickle-cell anaemia, e.g., if neurological complications are present.

title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Management - Longer-term management: Hydroxyurea
content: Hydroxyurea is used in the longer-term management of sickle-cell anaemia.

title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Management - Longer-term management: Hydroxyurea mechanism
content: Hydroxyurea increases HbF levels and is used in the prophylactic management of sickle-cell anaemia to prevent painful episodes.

title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Management - Longer-term management: Pneumococcal vaccine
content: Sickle-cell patients should receive the pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine every 5 years.

content: Analgesia, such as opiates, is part of the general management for sickle-cell crises.

title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Management: Rehydration
content: Rehydration is a general management step for sickle-cell crises.

content: Antibiotics should be considered in the management of sickle-cell crises if there is evidence of infection.

title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Management: Blood transfusion indications (Anaemia)
content: Blood transfusion is indicated in sickle-cell crises for severe or symptomatic anaemia.

title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Management: Blood transfusion indications (Pregnancy)
content: Blood transfusion is indicated in sickle-cell crises during pregnancy.

title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Management: Blood transfusion indications (Pre-operative)
content: Blood transfusion is indicated in sickle-cell crises pre-operatively.

title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Management: Blood transfusion (Hb S percentage)
content: During blood transfusion for sickle-cell crises, do not rapidly reduce the percentage of Hb S containing cells.

title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Management: Exchange transfusion indications (Acute vaso-occlusive crisis)
content: Exchange transfusion is indicated in sickle-cell crises for acute vaso-occlusive crisis (stroke, acute chest syndrome, multiorgan failure, splenic sequestration crisis).

title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Management: Exchange transfusion (Hb S percentage)
content: Exchange transfusion for sickle-cell crises aims to rapidly reduce the percentage of Hb S containing cells.

title: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura – Pathogenesis
content: Abnormally large and sticky multimers of von Willebrand's factor cause platelets to clump within vessels in Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP).

title: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura – ADAMTS13 deficiency
content: In Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP), there is a deficiency of ADAMTS13, a metalloprotease enzyme that breaks down large multimers of von Willebrand's factor.

title: G6PD deficiency – Definition and Epidemiology
content: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency is the commonest red blood cell enzyme defect. It is more common in people from the Mediterranean and Africa and is inherited in an X-linked recessive fashion.

title: G6PD deficiency – Precipitating factors
content: Many drugs can precipitate a crisis as well as infections and broad (fava) beans.

title: G6PD deficiency – G6PD role in pentose phosphate pathway
content: G6PD is the first step in the pentose phosphate pathway, which converts glucose-6-phosphate→ 6-phosphogluconolactone. This reaction also results in nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADP) → NADPH (glucose-6-phosphate + NADP → 6-phosphogluconolactone + NADPH).

title: G6PD deficiency – Role of NADPH and glutathione
content: NADPH is important for converting oxidized glutathione back to its reduced form. Reduced glutathione protects red blood cells from oxidative damage by oxidants such as superoxide anion (O2-) and hydrogen peroxide.

title: G6PD deficiency – Mechanism of oxidative stress
content: ↓ G6PD → ↓ reduced NADPH → ↓ reduced glutathione → increased red cell susceptibility to oxidative stress.

title: G6PD deficiency – Neonatal jaundice
content: Neonatal jaundice is often seen.

title: G6PD deficiency – Intravascular haemolysis
content: Intravascular haemolysis.

title: G6PD deficiency – Gallstones
content: Gallstones are common.

title: G6PD deficiency – Splenomegaly
content: Splenomegaly may be present.

title: G6PD deficiency – Blood film findings
content: Heinz bodies on blood films. Bite and blister cells may also be seen.

title: G6PD deficiency – Diagnostic test
content: Diagnosis is made by using a G6PD enzyme assay.

title: G6PD deficiency – Timing of G6PD enzyme assay
content: Levels should be checked around 3 months after an acute episode of hemolysis, RBCs with the most severely reduced G6PD activity will have hemolysed → reduced G6PD activity → not be measured in the assay → false negative results.

title: G6PD deficiency – Drugs causing haemolysis
content: Anti-malarials: primaquine. Ciprofloxacin. Sulph- group drugs: sulphonamides, sulphasalazine, sulfonylureas.

title: G6PD deficiency – Drugs thought to be safe
content: Penicillins. Cephalosporins. Macrolides. Tetracyclines. Trimethoprim.

title: G6PD deficiency – Gender and inheritance
content: G6PD deficiency: Male (X-linked recessive).

title: G6PD deficiency – Ethnicity
content: G6PD deficiency: African + Mediterranean descent.

title: G6PD deficiency – Typical history
content: G6PD deficiency: Neonatal jaundice, infection/drugs precipitate haemolysis, gallstones.

title: Essential thrombocytosis – Definition

title: Tranexamic acid – Definition
content: Tranexamic acid is a synthetic derivative of lysine.

title: Tranexamic acid – Mechanism of action
content: Tranexamic acid's primary mode of action is as an antifibrinolytic that reversibly binds to lysine receptor sites on plasminogen or plasmin. This prevents plasmin from binding to and degrading fibrin.

title: Tranexamic acid – Clinical use: Menorrhagia
content: Tranexamic acid is most commonly prescribed to help treat menorrhagia.

title: Tumour lysis syndrome – Definition
content: Tumour lysis syndrome (TLS) is a potentially deadly condition related to the treatment of high-grade lymphomas and leukaemias.

title: Tumour lysis syndrome – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Tumour lysis syndrome can occur in the absence of chemotherapy but is usually triggered by the introduction of combination chemotherapy. On occasion, it can occur with steroid treatment alone.

title: Tumour lysis syndrome – Pathophysiology
content: Tumour lysis syndrome occurs from the breakdown of the tumour cells and the subsequent release of chemicals from the cell.

title: Tumour lysis syndrome – Electrolyte abnormalities
content: Tumour lysis syndrome leads to a high potassium and high phosphate level in the presence of a low calcium.

title: Tumour lysis syndrome – Clinical suspicion
content: Tumour lysis syndrome should be suspected in any patient presenting with an acute kidney injury in the presence of a high phosphate and high uric acid level.

title: Tumour lysis syndrome – Prevention: IV fluids
content: IV fluids are used in the prevention of Tumour lysis syndrome.

title: Tumour lysis syndrome – Prevention: High-risk patients
content: Patients at higher risk of Tumour lysis syndrome should receive either allopurinol or rasburicase for prevention.

title: Tumour lysis syndrome – Rasburicase mechanism
content: Rasburicase is a recombinant version of urate oxidase, an enzyme that metabolizes uric acid to allantoin. Allantoin is much more water-soluble than uric acid and is, therefore, more easily excreted by the kidneys.

title: Tumour lysis syndrome – Rasburicase indication
content: Rasburicase is generally preferred now for patients at a higher risk of developing Tumour lysis syndrome.

title: Tumour lysis syndrome – Allopurinol indication
content: Allopurinol is generally used for patients in lower-risk groups for Tumour lysis syndrome.

title: Tumour lysis syndrome – Rasburicase and Allopurinol co-administration
content: Rasburicase and allopurinol should not be given together in the management of tumour lysis syndrome as this reduces the effect of rasburicase.

title: Tumour lysis syndrome – Cairo-Bishop scoring system
content: From 2004, Tumour lysis syndrome has been graded using the Cairo-Bishop scoring system.

title: Tumour lysis syndrome – Laboratory TLS criteria
content: Laboratory tumor lysis syndrome is defined by abnormality in two or more of the following, occurring within three days before or seven days after chemotherapy: uric acid > 475umol/l or 25% increase, potassium > 6 mmol/l or 25% increase, phosphate > 1.125mmol/l or 25% increase, calcium < 1.75mmol/l or 25% decrease.

title: Tumour lysis syndrome – Clinical TLS criteria
content: Clinical tumor lysis syndrome is defined as laboratory tumour lysis syndrome plus one or more of the following: increased serum creatinine (1.5 times upper limit of normal), cardiac arrhythmia or sudden death, seizure.

title: Von Willebrand's disease – Definition
content: Von Willebrand's disease is the most common inherited bleeding disorder.

title: Von Willebrand's disease – Inheritance
content: The majority of cases of Von Willebrand's disease are inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion.

title: Von Willebrand's disease – Clinical Features
content: Von Willebrand's disease characteristically behaves like a platelet disorder, with epistaxis and menorrhagia being common, whilst haemoarthroses and muscle haematomas are rare.

title: Von Willebrand's disease – Role of von Willebrand factor
content: Von Willebrand factor is a large glycoprotein which forms massive multimers up to 1,000,000 Da in size.

title: Von Willebrand's disease – Type 1
content: Type 1 Von Willebrand's disease involves a partial reduction in von Willebrand factor and accounts for 80% of patients.

title: Von Willebrand's disease – Type 2
content: Type 2 Von Willebrand's disease is characterized by an abnormal form of von Willebrand factor.

title: Von Willebrand's disease – Type 2A
content: Type 2A VWD is caused by defective platelet adhesion due to decreased high molecular weight VWF multimers (i.e. the VWF protein is too small).

title: Von Willebrand's disease – Type 2B
content: Type 2B VWD is characterised by a pathological increase of VWF-platelet interaction.

title: Von Willebrand's disease – Type 2M
content: Type 2M VWD is caused by a decrease in VWF-platelet interaction (not related to loss of high molecular weight multimers).

title: Von Willebrand's disease – Type 2N
content: Type 2N VWD is caused by abnormal binding of the VWF to Factor VIII.

title: Von Willebrand's disease – Type 3
content: Type 3 Von Willebrand's disease is the most severe form and involves a total lack of von Willebrand factor.

title: Von Willebrand's disease – Type 3 Inheritance
content: Type 3 von Willebrand's disease is inherited as an autosomal recessive trait.

title: Von Willebrand's disease – Investigations
content: Investigation for Von Willebrand's disease may show a prolonged bleeding time.

title: Von Willebrand's disease – Management
content: Tranexamic acid can be used for mild bleeding in Von Willebrand's disease.

title: Definition
content: Antiphospholipid syndrome is an acquired disorder characterised by a predisposition to both venous and arterial thromboses, recurrent fetal loss and thrombocytopenia. It may occur as a primary disorder or secondary to other conditions, most commonly systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).

title: Complications in Pregnancy
content: In pregnancy, the following complications may occur: recurrent miscarriage, IUGR, pre-eclampsia, placental abruption, pre-term delivery, and venous thromboembolism.
