title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Definition
content: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL) is a malignancy of precursor cells from the lymphocyte lineage, the most common of which is B-cell ALL.

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Epidemiology
content: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL) is the most common childhood malignancy.

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Clinical features
content: Any combination of persistent fever, pallor, unusual bleeding, lymphadenopathy and/or organomegaly should raise suspicions for Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Incidence
content: The incidence of Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia is 1.00 cases per 100,000 person-years.

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Peak Incidence Age
content: The peak incidence of Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia is between 1-5 years of age.

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Sex Ratio
content: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia is more common in males with a sex ratio of 1.5:1.

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Genetic Aetiology
content: An increased risk of developing Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia is observed among monozygotic twins and individuals with chromosomal abnormalities, including trisomy 21, Klinefelter's syndrome, and other inherited conditions with genetic instability, such as Fanconi anaemia.

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Viral Exposure Aetiology
content: Viral exposure is considered a contributing factor to the development of Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Environmental Aetiology
content: Environmental factors, including smoking or radiation exposure, are considered contributing factors to the development of Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Pathophysiology Definition
content: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL) is a haematological malignancy characterised by the clonal expansion of immature lymphoid precursors, known as lymphoblasts.

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Pathogenesis Overview
content: The pathogenesis of Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia involves a complex series of genetic, epigenetic, and microenvironmental alterations that disrupt normal haematopoiesis and immune function.

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Initial Genetic Events
content: The pathogenesis of Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia often begins with a somatic mutation in a progenitor cell within the bone marrow, leading to the formation of an aberrant clone of cells that proliferate uncontrollably.

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Fusion Genes in Pathogenesis
content: Common mutations observed in Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia involve rearrangements of BCR-ABL1, E2A-PBX1, and MLL genes, resulting in fusion proteins with increased or novel oncogenic activity.

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Transcription Factor Mutations
content: Mutations in transcription factors such as TAL1 and PAX5, critical for normal B-cell development, contribute to leukemogenesis by disrupting normal differentiation pathways in Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Tumour Suppressor Gene Mutations
content: Mutations in tumour suppressor genes such as TP53 and deletions in chromosomes 9 and 13 facilitate the survival and expansion of abnormal clones by preventing apoptosis in Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – DNA Methylation Changes
content: Changes in DNA methylation patterns can lead to the silencing of tumour suppressor genes in Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Histone Modifications
content: Histone modifications can alter chromatin structure and gene expression, contributing to the malignant phenotype in Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Microenvironmental Factors
content: The bone marrow microenvironment provides crucial support for leukemic cell survival and proliferation, influencing drug resistance and relapse in Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – WHO Classification
content: The World Health Organization (WHO) classification of Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia is based on immunophenotype, cytogenetics, and molecular genetics.

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – B-cell ALL
content: B-cell Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (B-ALL) accounts for approximately 85% of all ALL cases.

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – T-cell ALL
content: T-cell Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (T-ALL) accounts for approximately 15% of all ALL cases.

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Genetic Subtypes
content: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia is further classified into genetic subtypes based on recurrent cytogenetic abnormalities and molecular mutations, such as BCR-ABL1 fusion, ETV6-RUNX1 fusion, and KMT2A rearrangements.

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Clinical Presentation Overview
content: The clinical presentation of Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia is highly variable and depends on the extent of bone marrow infiltration and extramedullary involvement.

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Non-specific Clinical Presentation
content: Non-specific symptoms such as fatigue, fever, and weight loss are common in Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Organomegaly Presentation
content: Organomegaly, including hepatomegaly and splenomegaly, is frequently observed in Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Constitutional Fever
content: Fever (50%) is a common constitutional symptom in Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Fever due to Infection
content: Fever (50%) in Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia can also be due to infection secondary to neutropenia.

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Lymphadenopathy Presentation
content: Lymphadenopathy is present in 50% of Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia cases.

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Thrombocytopenia Manifestations
content: Unusual bleeding and bruising are common due to thrombocytopenia in Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Anaemia Manifestations
content: Anaemia in Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia presents with pallor, fatigue, and shortness of breath.

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Musculoskeletal Pain
content: Musculoskeletal pain, particularly bone and joint pain, is common in Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, affecting 25% of children.

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – CNS Involvement Headache
content: Headache and vomiting may indicate central nervous system (CNS) involvement in Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Testicular Enlargement
content: Testicular enlargement is a rare presentation of Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Mediastinal Mass Symptoms
content: A mediastinal mass in Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia can cause cough, dyspnoea, and superior vena cava obstruction.

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – FBC for Haematological Derangements
content: A full blood count (FBC) is required in suspected Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia cases to assess for haematological derangements.

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Thrombocytopenia on FBC
content: Thrombocytopenia is present in 75% of Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia cases.

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Anaemia on FBC
content: Anaemia is present in 75% of Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia cases.

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – WBC Count on FBC
content: White blood cell (WBC) count can be low, normal, or high in Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Low WBC Count Interpretation
content: A low white blood cell (WBC) count is present in 50% of Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia cases.

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Infection Screen
content: An infection screen is required in suspected Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia cases with fever to check for active infection.

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Coagulation Profile
content: A coagulation profile is required in suspected Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia cases to assess for any clotting derangements.

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Metabolic Panel for Complications
content: Urea, electrolytes, lactate dehydrogenase, and uric acid are required in suspected Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia cases to assess for complications such as tumour lysis syndrome.

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Diagnostic Requirements
content: Diagnosis of Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia requires examination of cell morphology and immunophenotyping; cytogenetics and molecular analysis are necessary for classification.

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Peripheral Blood Smear
content: A peripheral blood smear is always required to examine circulating lymphoblasts in the presence of an abnormal full blood count.

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Bone Marrow Aspiration
content: Bone marrow aspiration is a key investigation for Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia; a biopsy is only needed if insufficient cells are obtained.

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Lymph Node Biopsy
content: A lymph node biopsy, preferably excisional or needle over fine needle aspiration, is an early investigation in Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia if there is significant lymphadenopathy.

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Cerebrospinal Fluid Analysis
content: All children diagnosed with Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia undergo a lumbar puncture for cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis to assess for CNS involvement.

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Lymphoblast Identification in Morphology
content: Examination of samples in Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia may identify WBCs with characteristic morphological features of lymphoblasts, including large nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and scant cytoplasm.

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Normal Peripheral Smear Findings
content: Findings on a peripheral smear for Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia may be normal if leukaemia is still confined to the bone marrow.

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Diagnostic Threshold for Lymphoblasts
content: The most commonly accepted threshold for diagnosis of Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia is when lymphoblasts occupy >20% of bone marrow.

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Immunophenotyping for Diagnosis Confirmation
content: Immunophenotyping confirms the diagnosis of Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia by identifying common lymphoid antigens and features, and the absence of myeloid properties in abnormal cells.

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Immunophenotyping for Lineage Determination
content: Immunophenotyping determines whether Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia lymphoblasts are of B or T cell lineage through analysis of surface antigens.

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Cytogenetic and Molecular Analysis for Classification
content: Cytogenetic and molecular analysis is not required for diagnosis but is necessary to categorise Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia according to the WHO classification.

title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Techniques for Cytogenetic and Molecular Analysis
content: Identification of cytogenetic features in Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia involves chromosomal banding techniques and fluorescence in situ hybridisation (FISH), while various molecular techniques are used for characteristic molecular features.
